title: MS-CSI
text:
English   French
The MS-CSI project aims at exploring the relationships between lesion load quantified by MRI and the individual gait pattern (IGP) computed by the eGait device, which is a device jointly developed by the Department of Mathematics Jean Leray (LMJL) and the UmanIT company in Nantes, France.

title: MS-CSI
text:
Rationale
In the course of their lifetime, \(75\%\) of patients diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) complain about reduced mobility due to walking deficiencies. In clinical pratice, gait impairment is evaluated during the clinical exam using mainly three indicators:

The time required for a patient to walk twice a distance of \(25\) feet; this is the so-called Timed \(25\) Foot Walk (T25FW),
The walking perimeter of a patient, which is a part of the so-called EDSS score,
The cerebral and spinal lesion load, quantified by means of MR imaging.

These indicators however do not disentangle the various underlying forms of walking disabilities such as motor impairment, spacticity, equilibrium and so on.
The advent and development of connected devices offer a unique opportunity to collect non-invasive quantitative (and thus objective) data about a patient’s health, at minimal cost. The UmanIT company together with the Department of Mathematics Jean Leray (LMJL) have developed a medical device coined eGait paired with a statistical method that generates an individual gait pattern (IGP) using data collected by a motion sensor. The IGP represents the evolution of hip rotation during a typical walking cycle. The IGP represents an objective biomarker of gait impairment that is easily computed from data collected non-invasively and at minimal cost. The scientific hypothesis is that the IGP should share common information about gait impairment be competitive with other

title: MS-CSI
text:
Specific Aims
We focus in this project on the assessment of gait impairment. The original contributions are:

to propose a non-invasive low-cost medical device that generates an individual gait pattern for the patient during his/her clinical exam,
to study the statistical associations between the provided IGP and the lesion load obtained from the MRI data.

The project is build on mainly three specific aims:

Specific Aim 1

To evaluate the statistical associations between the IGP obtained from the sensor data and the lesion load obtained from the MRI data.

Specific Aim 2

To find group-level gait patterns using external sources of information such as lesion load provided by the MRI data or overall disability score provided by the EDSS data.

Specific Aim 3

To explain and predict the lesion load specific to a neuronal pathway or the membership to the previously determined groups, using the IGPs.

title: MS-CSI
text:
Methodology
Patients from the OFSEP-HD cohort that are seen in the University Hospital either in Nantes or Rennes will be wearing the eGait device during their T25FW test for obtaining their individual gait pattern (we predict \(100\) inclusions). As part of the standard protocol of this cohort, a number of demographic and clinical data will be collected as well. In addition, specific cutting-edge MRI sequences will be added as well for quantifying lesion load per neuronal pathway in both the brain and the spinal cord.

Methods for achieving SA1

Statistical data integration approaches will be used to explore the statistical association between IGP, clinical data and MRI data. These approaches are meant to integrate different heterogeneous data sources by separating the common and specific information they contain about the phenomenon under study.

Methods for achieving SA2

Clustering methods adapted for functional data will be used. Particular attention will be paid to semi-supervised approaches to account for clinical data and/or MRI data.

Methods for achieving SA3

Functional-on-functional regression models will be used for predicting lesion load from the IGP. Scalar-on-functional regression models and supervised classification methods will be used for predicting group membership from the IGP.


Chances are that none of the existing statistical approaches will be straightforwardly applicable to deal with our IGP. This is because the IGP is a functional data evaluating in the space of unit quaternion. As a result, a key aspect for achieving our SAs will be to adapt existing or create novel statistical methods that accommodate unit quaternion time series.

title: MS-CSI
text:
Expected Applications
The use of advanced cerebral and spinal MRI methods, not yet used in clinical practice, allows one to quantify lesion load at the granularity of the single neuronal pathway. We ambition:

to elaborate groupwise gait patterns (GGP) from the quantified lesion load obtained from the MRI data,
to facilitate the assessment of gait impairment for patients by matching his/her IGP to the closest GGP.

This work could have a significant impact since it could provide, during the clinical exam, a specific assessment of gait impairment. This would provide the neurologist with the means to propose dedicated follow-up at early onset of walking deficiencies or even possibly before any symptomatic discomfort. This would ultimately limit or delay aggravated walking deficiencies, which is one of the main fears reported by MS patients.

title: Aymeric Stamm
text:
Biography
I work as a research engineer in statistics at the National Center of Scientific Research (CNRS) in France. I am attached to the Department of Mathematics Jean Leray, a joint CNRS and Nantes University laboratory in Nantes, France. I am also a research fellow at the Computational Radiology Laboratory (CRL) affiliated to the Department of Radiology of Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, MA, USA.
I am an experienced statistician with focus on (i) the development of novel statistical methodologies for complex image analysis, with extensive but not exclusive application to magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and (ii) the extension of traditional statistical methods (estimation, inference, classification, regression) to the analysis of complex data (functions, Hilbertian, tensors, networks, densities, …).
I am also a research engineer with particular interest in making methods and algorithms developed in research labs available for use by a broader audience of applied fields. I am the author of several R packages available from my Github page (https://github.com/astamm).
I was awarded a B.Sc. degree in mathematical engineering from Ecole Centrale de Lyon (France) and a M.Sc. degree in mathematical engineering with major in statistics from Politecnico di Milano (Italy). During the course of my M.Sc., I collaborated with Dept. of Mathematics “F. Brioschi” (MOX) of the Politecnico di Milano and became co-investigator of the 2-year “Pn project” (2009-2010), whose objectives were to enable statistical inference from high-dimensional data. After my M.Sc., I obtained a Ph.D. degree in computer science. My Ph.D. focused on the development and application of statistical models for the study of the brain white matter microstructure and connectivity. During my first post-doctoral appointment at Harvard Medical School, I developed a statistical framework for MR image reconstruction that guarantees unbiasedness of the resulting composite complex MR image. I then joined again the Department of Mathematics of Politecnico di Milano where I pursued the development of novel statistical methodologies for complex image analysis and developed inferential tools for populations of densities and networks.
Simultaneously, I have been collaborating with the Dept. of Neuroradiology of the University Hospital of Rennes (France), since the beginning of my Ph.D., and with Dept. of Radiology of BCH (USA), since the beginning of my first post-doctoral appointment, to provide guidance on designing experiments and reviewing interim data, and to advise PIs of most of the Dept. projects on all statistical analysis methods and model development required in their projects. During my Ph.D., I also worked as a biostatistician at the Dept. of Epidemiology and Public Health of the University Hospital of Rennes (France) where I was in charge of the statistical analyses of several health-related projects (e.g., multiple sclerosis, practice of oral care in palliative care units).

Rotation data from the sensor






Unit quaternion


A unit quaternion \(\mathbf{q} = (q_w, q_x, q_y, q_z)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4\) encodes a rotation of angle \(\theta\) around the axis \(\mathbf{u}\) as: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{q} &= q_w + q_x \mathbf{i} + q_y \mathbf{j} + q_z \mathbf{k} \\
&= \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) + (u_x \mathbf{i} + u_y \mathbf{j} + u_z \mathbf{k}) \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right),
\end{aligned}
\] with \(\mathbf{i}^2 = \mathbf{j}^2 = \mathbf{k}^2 = \mathbf{i} \mathbf{j} \mathbf{k} = -1\).

Definition 1 (Smooth manifold) A smooth or differentiable manifold is a topological space that locally resembles linear space.






Figure 9: A manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) and the vector space \(T_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{M}\) tangent at point \(\mathcal{X}\). The velocity element \(\dot{\mathcal{X}}\) does not belong to the manifold but to the tangent space (Sola et al. 2018).

title: Analysis of 3D Object Orientation Trajectories
text:
Lie groups



Definition 2 (Group) A group is a set \(\mathcal{G}\), with composition operation \(\circ\), that, for elements \(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{Z} \in \mathcal{G}\), satisfies the following axioms:

Closure under \(\circ\): \(\mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{Y} \in \mathcal{G}\)
Identity \(\mathcal{E}\): \(\mathcal{E} \circ \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{E} = \mathcal{X}\)
Inverse \(\mathcal{X}^{-1}\): \(\mathcal{X}^{-1} \circ \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{X}^{-1} = \mathcal{E}\)
Associativity: \((\mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{Y}) \circ \mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X} \circ (\mathcal{Y} \circ \mathcal{Z})\)




Definition 3 (Lie group) A Lie group is a smooth manifold whose elements satisfy the group axioms.







Figure 10: Representation of a Lie group and its Lie algebra. The Lie algebra \(T_\mathcal{E} \mathcal{M}\) (red plane) is the tangent space to the Lie group \(\mathcal{M}\) (blue sphere) at the identity \(\mathcal{E}\) (Sola et al. 2018).

title: Analysis of 3D Object Orientation Trajectories
text:
Adding geometric invariants

The SRVF space is by construction invariant by position.

\[
d(\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2) = \| \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2 \|_{L^2}
\]

We can use suitable metrics to add further geometric invariants:








Geometric invariant
Distance (all isometric)




Warping
\(d(\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2) = \min_{\gamma \in \Gamma} \| \mathbf{v}_1 - (\mathbf{v}_2 \circ \gamma) \sqrt{\dot{\gamma}} \|_{L^2}\)


Orientation
\(d(\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2) = \min_{R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)} \| \mathbf{v}_1 - R \mathbf{v}_2 \|_{L^2}\)


Scale
\(d(\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2) = \left\| \frac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|_{L_2}} - \frac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|_{L_2}} \right\|_{L^2}\)



\[
\Gamma = \{ \gamma : [0,1] \to [0,1] | \gamma(0) = 0, \gamma(1) = 1, 0 < \dot{\gamma} < +\infty \}
\]

title: Analysis of 3D Object Orientation Trajectories
text:
Geometric invariants for 3D orientation trajectories







Reminder


In tangent space, we manipulate trajectories of the form:
\[
s \mapsto \theta(s) \mathbf{u}(s),
\]
where \(\theta\) is the rotation angle and \(\mathbf{u}\) the axis of rotation.













Rotation invariance


Makes two trajectories with orientations expressed in two different frames of reference equal. This is a good property.












Scale invariance


Makes two trajectories with proportional rotation angle equal. It might be a good property if proportional rotation angle captures differences due to individuals’ height.

Wrappin’ up







Elastic shape analysis for gait orientation data



We defined metric spaces to analyse gait orientation data using position, warping, rotation and possibly scale invariance.
We show their effectiveness in suppressing spurious variability.












The {squat} package


The {squat} package currently allows you to analyze trajectories of 3D object orientations:

seamlessly for clustering and PCA;
with a bit of extra work for other analyses (e.g. regression/prediction) via the provided exp() and log() maps.












Extension under elastic shape metrics


We aim to extend clustering, PCA and regression (prediction, classification) to make use of the elastic shape metric spaces.

title: fdacluster
text:
Clustering

Unlabeled data: observations are not assigned to pre-existing groups;
Goal: group together individuals or observations that share common features while ensuring the following property:

observations within a group must be as similar as possible,
observations between groups (belonging to different groups) must be as different as possible.

title: fdacluster
text:
Clustering methods



Centroid-based clustering


Clusters are represented by a central value or centroid. This centroid might not necessarily be one of the observations. These methods (e.g. k-means) operate in an iterative fashion in which the notion of similarity is derived by how close an observation is to the centroid of the cluster.






Hierarchical clustering


Observations that are closer in the data space are more related (similar) than observations that are far from each other. Clusters are formed by connecting observations according to their distance and clusters are allowed to be merged or splitted according to a cluster-based distance.






Density-based clustering


Search the data space for areas of high density of observations (e.g. DBSCAN). Clusters are defined as the areas of higher density within the data space compared to other regions. Observations in the sparse areas are usually considered to be noise and/or border points.
















A common ingredient


All methods but model-based rely on the ability to quantify closeness / distance between observations.

title: fdacluster
text:
Functional data - Notations

We consider a random variable \(X\) which takes values in \(F = \{ f: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{M} \}\).
The domain \(\mathcal{D}\) of the functions in \(F\) is a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\). Typically \(\mathcal{D} = \mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathcal{D} = [a, b]\).
The co-domain \(\mathcal{M}\) of the functions in \(F\) can be univariate or multivariate and can be either a Euclidean space or more generally a manifold. Typically, \(\mathcal{M} =
\mathbb{R}^p\).
The space \(F\) is equipped with a metric \(d\) so that \((F, d)\) is a metric space.

title: fdacluster
fdacluster
fdacluster
text:
The case \(\mathcal{D} = \mathbb{R}\)
In this situation, it is not possible to perform registration over \(\mathbb{R}\) and most of the time we use \(W\) to be the set of affine warping functions i.e. \(W = \{ h: h(t) = at+b \}\).
In this setting, it is tempting to equip \(F\) with the \(L^2\)-distance: \[
d_{L^2}^2(f, g) = \int_\mathbb{R} \left\| f(t) - g(t) \right\|_{\mathbb{R}^p}^2 dt.
\]
The \(L^2\)-distance is however not affine-invariant:
\[
d_{L^2}^2(f \circ h, g \circ h) = \frac{1}{a} d_{L^2}^2(f, g)
\]
A proper normalization can make it affine-invariant such as: \[
d(f, g) = \frac{d_{L^2}(f, g)}{\| f \|_{L^2} + \| g \|_{L^2}}
\]

title: fdacluster
text:
The case \(\mathcal{D} = [a, b]\)
In this situation, it is possible to perform registration over the set \(W\) of all boundary-preserving warping functions by using the square-root slope function (SRSF) framework (Tucker et al. 2013) under the assumption that all functions \(f \in F\) are absolutely continuous. In this case, the SRSF of a function \(f \in F\) which reads:
\[
\begin{array}{rccl}
q_f : & \mathbb{R} & \to & \mathbb{R}^p \\
& t & \mapsto & \frac{\dot{f}(t)}{\sqrt{ \| \dot{f}(t) \|_{\mathbb{R}^p} }},
\end{array}
\] is square-integrable and thus belong to \(L^2([a,b], \mathbb{R}^p)\).
We can therefore define: \[
d(f, g) = d_{L^2}(q_f, q_g),
\] and one can show that \(d\) is invariant under any boundary-preserving warping.

title: fdacluster
text:
Funct. \(k\)-means (Sangalli et al. 2010)



Initialization


Choose \(k\) initial observations as cluster centroids.






Align observations


Perform registration of all observed curves on each cluster centroid.






Assign observations to closest centroid


Assign each observed curve to the cluster with smallest distance to its center. This involves solving a constrained mixed integer and linear programming problem to ensure that no requested cluster will be empty.






Update cluster centroids


Recompute each cluster centroid given the newly assigned observations. Since the solution to the registration problem is not unique, the unique centroid is computed according to recommendations in Vantini (2012) to minimize total variation. If \(f_0\) is a computed centroid, then define the cluster centroid as \[
\widehat{f_0} = \arg \min_{f \in [f_0]} \sum_{i=1}^n d^2(f_i, f),
\] which is achieved for some warping function \(h^\star\) which needs to be further applied to all observations in that cluster.

title: fdacluster
text:
Funct. hierarchical clustering



Distance matrix computation


Compute the matrix \(D\) of pairwise distances between curves minimizing over the selected class \(W\) of warping functions.






Dendrogram computation


Apply traditional approaches to hierarchical clustering on \(D\) (either agglomerative or divisive) to build a hierarchy of possible clustering partitions of the data (dendrogram).






Assign observations to clusters



Cut the dendrogram to form \(k\) clusters and, in each cluster;
Register all curves to centroid via funct. \(1\)-mean clustering.







Update distance matrix


Update the distance matrix \(D\) using the registered curves from previous step with no further registration. This is used for final calculations of WSS and silhouettes.









Functional DBSCAN


Adapting DBSCAN to functional data follows the same principles.

title: The TDAverse
text:
What is topological data analysis?
Topology is a branch of mathematics at the interface of geometry and analysis.

Geometry is the study of rigid shapes (angle, curvature, distance).
Analysis is the study of limits (continuity, smoothness).
Topology is the study of properties of shapes that are invariant under continuous deformations: \[\text{Topology} \, = \, \text{Geometry} \,\, / \,\, \text{Analysis}\]

The core of Topological Data Analysis is persistent homology.

section: How can R users do TDA?
text:
How can R users do TDA?
We see (heretofore) R packages for TDA belonging to 3 types:

routine-specific

(ripserr, simplextree, kernelTDA, TDAvec)
analysis-specific

(TDAstats, TDApplied, ashapesampler, lookout)
general-purpose

(TDA, TDAkit, rgudhi)

Each meets certain needs, but they form a fragile ecosystem:



duplication of methods
hidden dependencies



sensitivity to upgrades
difficulty coupling

title: The TDAverse
text:
Design principles






Accessible


Empower users to learn and request.

Expressive names
Density of examples









Opinionated


Reduce burdens on collaborators & reviewers.

Evidence/practice-based defaults
Alert to any non-standard choices










Modular


Ease maintenance, contributions, and extensions.

Different packages for different tasks
Different packages for different steps









Interoperable


Reduce burdens on learners & programmers.

Unified structures & conventions
Co-extensions with other collections






These principles are inspired by those of other package collections and by our own experiences as enthusiasts, users, and developers in a niche area.

Distances between diagrams







Dependencies



Hera C++ library bundled within {phutil};
{BH} as a LinkingTo dependency for providing access to the Boost headers for built-in Hera compilation.
OpenMP for parallelization (optional; enabled at installation if available).












Implemented distances1





The \(p\)-Wasserstein distance: \(W_p^q (X, Y) = \inf_{\varphi : X \to Y} \left( \sum_{x \in X} \left\| x - \varphi(x) \right\|_q^p \right)^{1/p}\)
The bottleneck distance: \(W_\infty^q (X, Y) = \inf_{\varphi : X \to Y} \left( \sup_{x \in X} \left\| x - \varphi(x) \right\|_q \right)\)

where \(X\) and \(Y\) are two persistence diagrams, \(\varphi\) is a bijection between the points of \(X\) and \(Y\) (including points on the diagonal), and \(\| \cdot \|_q\) is the \(q\)-norm in the plane.
Available functions: bottleneck_distance(), wasserstein_distance(), bottleneck_pairwise_distances and wasserstein_pairwise_distances().

text:
Data acquisition and modeling





Imaging parameters









Fick et al. (2019)


\[
\mathbf{q} = \frac{\gamma \delta G}{2 \pi} \mathbf{n}
\]

\(\gamma\): gyromagnetic ratio;
\(\delta\): gradient duration;
\(G\): gradient amplitude;
\(\mathbf{n}\): gradient direction.








Sensitivity to microstructure


Freely diffusing water:
\[ S(\mathbf{q}) = S_0 \exp \left( - b D \right) \]
with \(b = \gamma^2 \delta^2 G^2 \left( \Delta - \frac{\delta}{3} \right)\).

An R6-based package

#' Base compartment class
#'
#' @description The base class for compartment models.
#'
#' @keywords internal
BaseCompartment <- R6::R6Class(
  "BaseCompartment",
  public = list(
    #' @description Computes the signal attenuation predicted by the model.
    #'
    #' @param small_delta A numeric value specifying the duration of the
    #'   gradient pulse in milliseconds.
    #' @param big_delta A numeric value specifying the duration between the
    #'   gradient pulses in milliseconds.
    #' @param G A numeric value specifying the strength of the gradient in
    #'   mT.\eqn{\mu}m\eqn{^{-1}}.
    #' @param direction A numeric vector specifying the direction of the
    #'   gradient. Defaults to `c(0, 0, 1)`.
    #' @param echo_time A numeric value specifying the echo time in
    #'   milliseconds.
    #' @param n_max An integer value specifying the maximum order of the Bessel
    #'   function. Defaults to `20L`.
    #' @param m_max An integer value specifying the maximum number of extrema
    #'   for the Bessel function. Defaults to `50L`.
    #'
    #' @return A numeric value storing the predicted signal attenuation.
    #'
    #' @examples
    #' freeComp <- FreeCompartment$new()
    #' freeComp$get_signal(small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30, G = 0.040)
    #'
    #' sphereComp <- SphereCompartment$new()
    #' sphereComp$get_signal(small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30, G = 0.040)
    #'
    #' sodermanComp <- SodermanCompartment$new()
    #' sodermanComp$get_signal(small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30, G = 0.040)
    #'
    #' staniszComp <- StaniszCompartment$new()
    #' staniszComp$get_signal(small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30, G = 0.040)
    #'
    #' neumanComp <- NeumanCompartment$new()
    #' neumanComp$get_signal(
    #'   small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30, G = 0.040,
    #'   echo_time = 40
    #' )
    #'
    #' callaghanComp <- CallaghanCompartment$new()
    #' callaghanComp$get_signal(small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30, G = 0.040)
    #'
    #' vanGelderenComp <- VanGelderenCompartment$new()
    #' vanGelderenComp$get_signal(small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30, G = 0.040)
    get_signal = function(small_delta, big_delta, G,
                          direction = c(0, 0, 1),
                          echo_time = NULL,
                          n_max = 20L,
                          m_max = 50L) {
      private$compute_signal(
        small_delta = small_delta,
        big_delta = big_delta,
        G = G,
        direction = direction,
        echo_time = echo_time,
        n_max = n_max,
        m_max = m_max
      )
    },

    #' @description Returns the names of the compartment parameters
    #'
    #' @return A character vector storing the names of the compartment
    #'   parameters.
    #'
    #' @examples
    #' freeComp <- FreeCompartment$new()
    #' freeComp$get_parameter_names()
    get_parameter_names = function() {
      names(private$parameters())
    },

    #' @description Returns the values of the compartment parameters
    #'
    #' @return A numeric vector storing the values of the compartment
    #'   parameters.
    #'
    #' @examples
    #' freeComp <- FreeCompartment$new()
    #' freeComp$get_parameters()
    get_parameters = function() {
      private$parameters()
    }
  )
)

Should faciliate implementation of new compartment models.

These guidelines are meant to be followed during the live setup block at the start of the term, but also work standalone if you come to class with an already-configured machine (skip ahead). We target latest stable versions of everything.
This page covers the parts of the toolchain common to both ENSAI courses: R, the Positron IDE, Ubuntu specifics, and the core R packages. If you are also taking the Reproducible Workflows course, continue with the companion Setup · Reproducible Workflows page for Quarto, Python, git and publishing.

title: Setup your machine · common
text:
1. Install R
R is the language itself. Download the installer for your OS and follow the instructions:

macOS / Windows: https://cran.r-project.org
Linux (Ubuntu): follow the Ubuntu section below rather than using the generic link.

Check it works:
R.version.string   # e.g. "R version 4.6.1"

title: Setup your machine · common
text:
2. Install Positron (the IDE)
Positron is a next-generation data science IDE (a data-science-flavoured fork of VS Code) that runs both R and Python.

Download: https://positron.posit.co/download.html
Choose the arm64 / x86_64 build that matches your machine.

Open Positron. On first launch it will offer to install the R extensions and detect your R installation. Confirm both.
Positron will use Quarto automatically for the Quarto preview/render.

title: Setup your machine · common
text:
3. Linux (Ubuntu)
If you run Ubuntu, install the applications above from their .deb binaries, then set up R packages. Two routes are available for packages: the fast, recommended r2u binaries, or a manual compile-from-source fallback. Both are detailed below.

3.1 Install R and Positron from .deb files
Download the .deb installer for each of R and Positron from their respective sites (choose the arm64 build on an ARM, Apple-Silicon-style machine, or x86_64 otherwise). Then install them together and let apt pull in any missing dependencies:
sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/*.deb     # adjust the path to where you saved the files
sudo apt --fix-broken install
The second command is the important clean-up step: dpkg -i itself does not install dependency packages, so it will often report missing dependencies, which apt --fix-broken install then resolves. If you prefer, a plain sudo apt install -f works the same.
For R alone you do not have to use the CRAN .deb at all. If you prefer your package manager, install r-base (and r-base-dev) from the Ubuntu or CRAN apt repository afterwards with sudo apt install r-base r-base-dev instead. Either way you do not need RStudio: Positron is the IDE, and it talks to whatever R binary sits on your PATH.


3.2 Recommended: install R packages via r2u (Ubuntu binaries)
r2u is a project that builds almost all of CRAN (currently about 25,000 packages) into Ubuntu binary .deb packages and serves them as an apt repository. With a small companion called bspm, your ordinary install.packages("tidyverse") transparently installs prebuilt Ubuntu binaries in seconds, with no compilation and no manual wiring of system libraries. This removes precisely the libcurl/fontconfig/harfbuzz… laundry list that makes a source install painful.
Scope and caveats:

It targets Ubuntu LTS releases (22.04 “jammy”, 24.04 “noble”, 26.04 “resolute”) on amd64, with arm64 supported on 24.04 and 26.04. It is not for other distributions.
Installing via bspm needs sudo: it writes into the system R library.
Project-pinned environments such as the uvr projects you build later in the Reproducible Workflows course do not go through bspm; they manage their own project-local library. So keep the build tools from the fallback below even if you use r2u.

Set it up (condensed from the official guide):
# 1. fetch the signing key
sudo apt update
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends wget ca-certificates gnupg
gpg --homedir /tmp --no-default-keyring \
    --keyring /usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg \
    --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com \
    --recv-keys A1489FE2AB99A21A 67C2D66C4B1D4339 51716619E084DAB9

# 2. register the r2u apt repository (adjust 'noble' to your Ubuntu release:
#    jammy, noble or resolute; use `lsb_release -cs` to print it)
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg] https://r2u.stat.illinois.edu/ubuntu noble main" \
    | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/r2u.list
sudo apt update

# 3. python pieces bspm needs, then bspm itself
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends python3-{dbus,gi,apt}
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("bspm")'

# 4. enable bspm for every R session
sudo bash -c 'echo "suppressMessages(bspm::enable())" >> "$(R RHOME)/etc/Rprofile.site"'
From then on, inside Positron’s R console, the normal command just works and pulls binaries:
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)


3.3 Fallback: compile from source
Use this route if your Ubuntu release is not covered by r2u, you do not want a system-wide (sudo) install, or a package you need is not in r2u. Compiling the tidyverse from source needs both a C/C++ toolchain and the header files of the system libraries several of its packages link against. Install them all at once:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y \
  r-base r-base-dev cmake \
  libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libfontconfig1-dev \
  libharfbuzz-dev libfribidi-dev libfreetype6-dev libpng-dev \
  libjpeg-dev
(on 24.04 “noble” the JPEG/TIFF library is libtiff6-dev; on 22.04 “jammy” and older it is libtiff5-dev, so append the one matching your release).
Then, still in the terminal, install pak (a modern, fast package manager that also helps resolve these build issues) and use it from the R console:
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("pak")'
pak::pak("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
Unlike the r2u path (3.2) where plain install.packages() pulls prebuilt binaries, here pak actually compiles from source, but it does the dependency bookkeeping for you and caches the compiled result, so a later reinstallation is quick.

title: Setup your machine · common
text:
4. Install R packages
Open the R console in Positron and run:
install.packages("tidyverse")   # the core data-science collection
On Ubuntu with r2u set up (section 3.2), this command automatically installs Ubuntu binaries, so you do not need pak or the manual toolchain. On macOS/Windows the installer handles everything for you.
A note on the two commands you will meet in this guide:

install.packages() is the R-basics installer. With r2u (+bspm) running it installs Ubuntu binaries, which is why it is the default here.
pak::pak() is an optional third-party package manager with better dependency resolution and caching, and can also install straight from GitHub or a local folder. It does not go through r2u, so on the r2u path it offers no speed advantage. Reach for it when a package is not (yet) on CRAN, or to compile from source as in the fallback (section 3.3).

Verify with:
library(tidyverse)
You should see the package startup message listing dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, forcats.
By the time of the Reproducible Workflows course you will additionally want:
install.packages(c("janitor", "naniar", "skimr", "gt", "palmerpenguins", "withr", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "pins", "usethis", "gitcreds"))
(pins for data pinning; withr scopes options like random-number seeds so a render is reproducible; janitor/naniar/skimr feed the data-cleaning and EDA labs; gt formats report tables; palmerpenguins ships the penguins data used by the session-1 labs; usethis and gitcreds drive the Session 2/3 git work, including the GitHub personal-access-token setup in the Reproducible Workflows setup. All of these are available as r2u binaries too, so the same plain install.packages() call above works unchanged on the r2u path. Pinning the R and package versions of a project is done with uvr (see the Reproducible Workflows setup), not installed here.)

title: Setup your machine · common
text:
5. Some worthy Positron extensions (optional)

Air: A Visual Studio Code extension for Air, an R formatter and language server, written in Rust.
Jarl: A Visual Studio Code extension for Jarl, a fast R linter.
Posit Assistant: An AI assistant for Positron. It uses functionality that is available only in Positron, so it will not work with other VS Code forks, like Cursor or Windsurf.
Pyrefly: The Pyrefly extension uses Pyrefly to provide language server features for Python in VS Code. Please see https://pyrefly.org for more information.
Quarto: A Visual Studio Code extension for the Quarto scientific and technical publishing system.
Shiny: This is an extension to help launch Shiny applications. Shiny is a package for Python and R that is designed to make it easy to build interactive web applications with the powerful data and scientific features of Python and R.

Some of them are pre-installed with Positron; others require opt-in installs via the Extensions panel.

title: Setup your machine · common
text:
6. Version checks, all together
For these courses we will use R, Quarto and git. Check all three at once.
In the R console:
R.version.string            # the R version, e.g. "R version 4.6.1"
and in a terminal:
quarto --version            # e.g. 1.10.x
git --version               # e.g. 2.4x.x
(If you also set up Python with uv for the Reproducible Workflows course, uv --version confirms that too.)
If everything reports a version, you are ready. Ask the instructor for help if any step errors; resolve these at the start so the labs run smoothly.

text:
Getting the data
The data is sourced by code from an open-data portal of your choice. Because the download lives inside the document, it is recorded in the analysis itself; anyone who re-renders this document gets the same data and the same results. Record the dataset’s publisher and URL in the text so the provenance is explicit.
The only portal-specific part is the fetch. This template shows two ways; use the one that fits your portal:

{rdatagouv} (data.gouv.fr only, optional): search/download from R.
Any portal by URL: download.file() works with any portal’s direct download link.


# Load what you use. {rdatagouv} only if you're on data.gouv.fr and want it.
# library(rdatagouv)    # search / download datasets from data.gouv.fr
library(janitor)        # clean column names, tabulate with tabyl()
library(naniar)         # visualise missing values

What does reproducible mean?
section: 1.2 What research is: the IMRAD structure
text:
1.2 What research is: the IMRAD structure
Research, distilled, is a short chain of steps:


A question worth asking.
An experiment (or study) that collects data to answer it.
Analysis methods, explained and applied to that data.
Results presented and commented.
A discussion that puts the results and the original question into perspective.


That is, in essence, what data science does every day: it turns step 2’s data into step 4’s results by doing step 3 (analysis) with code, statistics and visualization.

That structure is often called IMRAD: introduction, methods, results and discussion. Reproducibility means shipping the implementation details of every one of these steps, so a reader can rebuild them from scratch.


markdown## What research is: the IMRAD structure {.inv}

Research, distilled, is a short chain of steps:

::: {}

1. A **question** worth asking.
2. An **experiment** (or study) that collects **data** to answer it.
3. **Analysis** methods, explained *and* applied to that data.
4. **Results** presented and commented.
5. A **discussion** that puts the results and the original question into perspective.
:::

**That is, in essence, what data science does every day**: it turns step 2's data into step 4's results by doing step 3 (analysis) with code, statistics and visualization.

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
That structure is often called **IMRAD**: introduction, methods, results and discussion. Reproducibility means shipping the *implementation details* of every one of these steps, so a reader can rebuild them from scratch.
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
2.1 The reproducibility crisis
John Ioannidis’s 2005 paper, Why Most Published Research Findings Are False, used a mathematical model to show that most claimed findings are false positives: the spark of the modern reproducibility crisis.







Core concepts of the crisis



The 2005 paper: small samples, tiny effects, high bias, flexible designs make claimed findings statistically likely to be wrong.
Impact across fields: from medicine and biomedicine into psychology, the social sciences and the life sciences.












Key causes



“Publish or perish” culture: novelty rewarded over truth.
P-hacking: adjusting analysis until a result becomes significant.
Publication bias: positive results favored over negative or null findings.
Nothing shared: no data, code or protocol.






markdown## The reproducibility crisis {.inv}

John Ioannidis's [2005
paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1182327/pdf/pmed.0020124.pdf), *Why Most Published Research Findings Are False*, used a mathematical model to show that most claimed findings are false positives: the spark of the modern reproducibility crisis.

::: {.callout-tip title="Core concepts of the crisis"}
- The 2005 paper: small samples, tiny effects, high bias, flexible designs make claimed findings statistically likely to be wrong.
- Impact across fields: from medicine and biomedicine into psychology, the social sciences and the life sciences.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Key causes"}
- "Publish or perish" culture: novelty rewarded over truth.
- P-hacking: adjusting analysis until a result becomes significant.
- Publication bias: positive results favored over negative or null findings.
- Nothing shared: no data, code or protocol.
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
2.2 “Works here” vs “works anywhere”
The test is simple. Take an analysis you did last month and ask three questions:


Will it re-run?: does the code execute from source, with no hidden clicks or hand-fixes?
Will it re-run here?: does it reproduce on your machine tomorrow, when packages have updated?
Will it re-run anywhere?: does it reproduce on a colleague’s machine, or in a year?



Everything in this course is in service of making each “will it re-run?” an unequivocal yes: for you, and for anyone else.


markdown## "Works here" vs "works anywhere" {.inv}

The test is simple. Take an analysis you did last month and ask three questions:

::: {.spread}
1. **[Will it re-run?]{.green}**: does the code execute from source, with no hidden clicks or hand-fixes?

2. **[Will it re-run *here*?]{.amber}**: does it reproduce on *your* machine tomorrow, when packages have updated?

3. **[Will it re-run *anywhere*?]{.indigo}**: does it reproduce on a colleague's machine, or in a year?
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Everything in this course is in service of making each "will it re-run?" an unequivocal **yes**: for you, and for anyone else.
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
2.3 What breaks reproducibility
The enemies we’ll learn to fight, one per later session:


The human memory gap: “I clicked through the setup”, “I cleaned it by hand in Excel”. Code that lives nowhere but the analyst’s head.
The moving environment: install.packages() happily updates globally, so your analysis breaks when a dependency version silently changes.
The (dis)appearing data: reading a local file path only you have; data that can’t be re-downloaded.
The vanished machine: your laptop dies, your setup is gone.



The reproducibility habit answers all four at once: document your code, pin your environment, source your data, version everything.


markdown## What breaks reproducibility {.inv}

The enemies we'll learn to fight, one per later session:

::: {}
- **[The human memory gap]{.green}**: "I clicked through the setup", "I cleaned it by hand in Excel". Code that lives nowhere but the analyst's head.

- **[The moving environment]{.amber}**: `install.packages()` happily updates *globally*, so your analysis breaks when a dependency version silently changes.

- **[The (dis)appearing data]{.indigo}**: reading a local file path only you have; data that can't be re-downloaded.

- **[The vanished machine]{.indigo}**: your laptop dies, your setup is gone.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
The *reproducibility habit* answers all four at once: **document your code, pin your environment, source your data, version everything.**
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
2.4 What reproducible research looks like
Here is the shape of every analysis we build this course:


Data is sourced by code (a documented package, an open-data portal), never by manual download.
The analysis lives in a document (Quarto) that mixes prose and code, so seeing the result shows how it was made.
Dependencies are pinned (uvr/uv, or renv), so the document re-runs tomorrow.
Everything is versioned with git: every change, every step, reversible.
It is published to a URL others can reach.



You already learned the R side: vectors, data frames, plotting. This course wraps that skill in a workflow so your results can be trusted, shared and rebuilt by anyone, anywhere.


markdown## What reproducible research looks like {.inv}

Here is the shape of every analysis we build this course:

::: {}

1. **Data** is **sourced** by code (a documented package, an open-data portal), never by manual download.
2. The **analysis lives in a document** (Quarto) that mixes prose and code, so *seeing* the result shows *how* it was made.
3. **Dependencies are pinned** (`uvr`/`uv`, or `renv`), so the document re-runs tomorrow.
4. **Everything is versioned** with git: every change, every step, reversible.
5. **It is published** to a URL others can reach.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
You already learned the R side: vectors, data frames, plotting. This course wraps that skill in a **workflow** so your results can be *trusted, shared and rebuilt by anyone, anywhere.*
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
2.5 The course at a glance
Over three sessions we climb from “it works on my machine” to “it’s published and reproducible”:


Session 1 · Write: your first Quarto documents: prose + code + results, transparent from source.
Session 2 · Source: source an open-data set (e.g. data.gouv.fr), pin it, version it with git, and start your portfolio book.
Session 3 · Publish: deepen git (pull requests, review), manage deps with uvr/uv, publish to Posit Connect, and finish Chapter 1.



By the end you’ll have a published, versioned, reproducible portfolio: and the habit of making every future analysis reproducible by default. Projects in other courses slot into the same book, so your portfolio grows over time.


markdown## The course at a glance {.inv}

Over three sessions we climb from "it works on my machine" to "it's published and reproducible":

::: {}
- **[Session 1 · Write]{.green}**: your first Quarto documents: prose + code + results, transparent from source.

- **[Session 2 · Source]{.amber}**: source an open-data set (e.g. data.gouv.fr), *pin* it, **version it with git**, and start your **portfolio book**.

- **[Session 3 · Publish]{.indigo}**: deepen git (pull requests, review), manage deps with **uvr/uv**, publish to **Posit Connect**, and finish Chapter 1.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
**By the end you'll have a published, versioned, reproducible portfolio**: and the habit of making every future analysis reproducible by default. Projects in other courses slot into the same book, so your portfolio grows over time.
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
3.3 Think in terms of projects
Open your course folder as a project and work there: the working directory is that folder.

Every file path in R is resolved relative to your working directory unless you write an absolute one. A small, predictable layout keeps a project tidy:

# a tidy project layout
my-project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
└── scripts/




In Positron, open the folder as a project (File → Open Folder); a relative path like read_csv("data/raw/penguins.csv") then just works.
Prefer relative paths: they let a script run on any machine with the same folder layout.
Projects are the unit you’ll version, pin and publish in Sessions 2–3.



Thinking in projects, not loose files, is the first reproducibility habit: it makes your work portable, and it’s the container everything else (git, uvr, publishing) builds on.

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
4.1 What is a Quarto document?
A .qmd file is plain text that mixes three things:

Markdown for prose: headings, lists, emphasis, links, just like a README.
Code cells that run R or Python when the document renders, with their output (numbers, figures, tables) written into the document.
YAML front matter at the top (title, format, …) controlling how the whole thing is rendered.


Render it once (quarto render, or Preview in Positron) and you get a self-contained report: the story and the evidence, generated from the same source.


markdown## What is a Quarto document? {.inv}

A **`.qmd`** file is plain text that mixes three things:

::: {.spread}
[**Markdown for prose**]{.green}: headings, lists, emphasis, links, just like a README.

[**Code *cells***]{.amber} that run R or Python when the document renders, with their output (numbers, figures, tables) written **into** the document.

[**YAML front matter**]{.indigo} at the top (`title`, `format`, …) controlling how the whole thing is rendered.
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
Render it once (`quarto render`, or *Preview* in Positron) and you get a **self-contained report**: the story *and* the evidence, generated from the same source.
:::

text:
4.3 The YAML header
YAML is the control panel at the top of every document:
---
title: "My first report"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---


title, author: metadata shown at the top of the page.
format: what to build, html, pdf, docx, revealjs (these slides are a revealjs), or a whole book (Session 2).
Many more options: themes, table of contents, captions…



YAML uses strict key: value pairs with two-space indentation. Indentation mistakes are the single most common Quarto error: the error message points at the line. Full options: Front matter · formats: All formats.


markdown## The YAML header {.inv}

YAML is the control panel at the top of every document:

```yaml
---
title: "My first report"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---
```

::: {}

- `title`, `author`: metadata shown at the top of the page.
- `format`: what to build, `html`, `pdf`, `docx`, `revealjs` (these slides are a `revealjs`), or a whole **book** (Session 2).
- Many more **options**: themes, table of contents, captions…
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
YAML uses strict *key: value* pairs with two-space indentation. Indentation mistakes are the single most common Quarto error: the error message points at the line. Full options: [Front matter](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/front-matter.html) · formats: [All formats](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html).
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
4.4 Code cells: controlling what shows
An option is a #| comment on its own line inside the cell, e.g. #| echo: false:



Option
Effect




label: fig-… / label: tbl-…
cross-reference a figure or table


eval: false
keep the code, don’t run it


echo: false
hide the code, show the output


include: false
show neither (setup code)


fig-cap: "…" / tbl-cap: "…"
caption a figure or table


message/warning: false
silence package-load chatter




By default a cell shows code + output; each #| option changes that. The full list: Code execution options.


markdown## Code cells: controlling what shows {.inv}

An **option** is a `#|` comment on its own line inside the cell, e.g. `#| echo: false`:

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `label: fig-…` / `label: tbl-…` | cross-reference a figure or table |
| `eval: false` | keep the code, don't run it |
| `echo: false` | hide the *code*, show the output |
| `include: false` | show neither (setup code) |
| `fig-cap: "…"` / `tbl-cap: "…"` | caption a figure or table |
| `message/warning: false` | silence package-load chatter |

::: {.callout-desc}
By default a cell shows **code + output**; each `#|` option changes that. The full list: [Code execution options](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html).
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
4.5 One tool, many languages
Quarto is language-agnostic: the same .qmd renders R, Python, or both.


An R cell and a Python cell sit side by side in one document, each with the same options.
Which language to use is a property of each cell, not of the document.
R and Python dominate in data science, but Quarto also speaks Julia and Observable JS, plus more via Jupyter.
Your portfolio (Session 2) is Python-compatible by design: prose plus whichever language fits the analysis.



Render once and you get a single self-contained report, whatever the language. That portability is why this course’s toolchain covers both R and Python.


markdown## One tool, many languages {.inv}

Quarto is **language-agnostic**: the same `.qmd` renders R, Python, or both.

::: {}

- An R cell and a Python cell sit side by side in one document, each with the same options.
- Which language to use is a property of each **cell**, not of the document.
- R and Python dominate in data science, but Quarto also speaks [**Julia and Observable JS**](https://quarto.org/docs/faq/#what-programming-languages-are-supported-in-quarto), plus more via Jupyter.
- Your portfolio (Session 2) is **Python-compatible by design**: prose plus whichever language fits the analysis.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Render once and you get a single *self-contained report*, whatever the language. That portability is why this course's toolchain covers both R and Python.
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
4.6 A Quarto document in action
Everything so far is easier to see than to describe. Try it for yourself:


Open the document you just created in Positron.
Press Preview (or Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+K) to render it.
Change a heading or a number, save, re-render, and the output updates to match the source.



The loop, edit source → render → see output, is the whole of Quarto. Everything else (figures, books, publishing) is that loop scaled up.


markdown## A Quarto document in action {.inv}

Everything so far is easier to *see* than to describe. Try it for yourself:

::: {.spread}
- Open the document you just created in Positron.
- Press **Preview** (or Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+K) to render it.
- Change a heading or a number, save, re-render, and the output updates to match the source.
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
The loop, **edit source → render → see output**, is the whole of Quarto. Everything else (figures, books, publishing) is that loop scaled up.
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
text:
5.1 Literate programming
The idea at the heart of Quarto (prose and code woven together) has a name:


Literate programming (Knuth, 1984): an analysis document is written primarily for humans to read, with the code embedded so the results it discusses appear in place.
The reader follows your thinking; the machine follows your instructions.
The document is self-documenting: the evidence sits beside the claim it supports.



Contrast with the output-first habit: a completed PDF with no source is only half an analysis. Here, the source is the analysis.


markdown## Literate programming {.inv}

The idea at the heart of Quarto (**prose *and* code woven together**) has a name:

::: {}

- **Literate programming** (Knuth, 1984): an analysis document is written primarily for *humans to read*, with the *code embedded* so the results it discusses appear in place.
- The reader follows your *thinking*; the machine follows your *instructions*.
- The document is **self-documenting**: the evidence sits beside the claim it supports.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Contrast with the *output-first* habit: a completed PDF with no source is only half an analysis. Here, the **source is the analysis**.
:::

title: What does reproducible mean?
section: 5.2 Structure a report for a reader
text:
5.2 Structure a report for a reader
A reproducible report is a document, not a dump of output. Structure it:


Question first: what are you asking, in one sentence?
Data: where it came from, how it was sourced (the code shows this).
Cleaning decisions: what you renamed, recoded, dropped, and why.
Figures & tables: each captioned and referred to in the text.
Findings: what you found, honestly, limits included.



The caption habit. A figure without a caption is a picture; a captioned figure referred to in prose is evidence. You’ll practice this in Lab 2 and it becomes the backbone of your portfolio chapter.


markdown## Structure a report for a reader {.inv}

A reproducible report is a *document*, not a dump of output. Structure it:

::: {}

1. **Question first**: what are you asking, in one sentence?
2. **Data**: where it came from, how it was sourced (the code shows this).
3. **Cleaning decisions**: what you renamed, recoded, dropped, and *why*.
4. **Figures & tables**: each **captioned** and *referred to in the text*.
5. **Findings**: what you found, honestly, limits included.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
**The caption habit.** A figure without a caption is a picture; a captioned figure *referred to in prose* is evidence. You'll practice this in Lab 2 and it becomes the backbone of your portfolio chapter.
:::

5.6 The transparency loop
Because source is the analysis, any reader can ask “how did you make that?” and get a real answer.


This deck ships with a code popover: press c on any slide to see the source behind it.
That’s the habit we want you to internalize for your own work: the analysis answers its own “how”.
When someone asks “where does this number come from?”, the answer is “render the document”, not “from my head”.

text:
6.2 The semester plan
Here’s how your book fills up over the term:


Session 1 (today): you learn the document mechanics; the book scaffold renders.
Session 2: you source a dataset by code (any open-data portal, data.gouv.fr or your own country’s), clean it, and drop your EDA into Chapter 1.
Session 3: you put the book under git, pin it with renv/uv, and publish it.
Later courses: other instructors slot their work into the placeholder chapters, so the book keeps growing.



By semester’s end you hold a published, versioned, reproducible portfolio, and the skill to do it again for any analysis.

text:
2.2 The pipe: |>
The pipe |> sends the value on its left into the first argument of the function on its right:

The pipe: top-to-bottom
penguins |>                                        # raw data set
  dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie") |>            # keep only Adelie penguins
  dplyr::mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) # compute a new column

Reads: penguins, THEN filter(…). One line per data processing step: easy to comment/read.

The nested equivalent: inside-out
filtered_penguins <- dplyr::filter(penguins, species == "Adelie")
dplyr::mutate(filtered_penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)


The pipe keeps your script readable top-to-bottom; the nested alternative reads inside-out. The backbone of data work: one rule, the data always goes first.


markdown## The pipe: `|>` {.inv}

The pipe `|>` sends the value on its left into the *first argument* of the function on its right:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
The pipe: top-to-bottom
```r
penguins |>                                        # raw data set
  dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie") |>            # keep only Adelie penguins
  dplyr::mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) # compute a new column
```
:::

Reads: penguins, THEN filter(...). One line per data processing step: easy to comment/read.

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
The nested equivalent: inside-out
```r
filtered_penguins <- dplyr::filter(penguins, species == "Adelie")
dplyr::mutate(filtered_penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)
```
:::

::: {.paper-card}
The pipe keeps your script readable **top-to-bottom**; the nested alternative reads inside-out. The backbone of data work: one rule, **the data always goes first**.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

::: {.codewindow}

```{r}
  # keep penguins with body mass ≥ 4000 g

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
```

text:
3.1 Why plot?
A plot is the fastest way to feel your data. Anscombe’s quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike.










The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the plots tell them apart. A table could not, a hist() of a single column would not, an illustration does.

The lesson. Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of Exploratory Data Analysis.



markdown## Why plot? {.inv}

A plot is the fastest way to *feel* your data. Anscombe's quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike.

::: {.split-2}
```{r}
#| label: anscombe
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.8
par(bg = "white")                 # opaque white figure so the black ink shows on the dark slide
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 2, 1), cex = 0.8)
for (i in 1:4) {
  plot(anscombe[, c(2*i - 1, 2*i)], pch = 19, col = "#2E7D6B",
       main = paste0("Dataset ", i))
}
```

The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the *plots* tell them apart. A table could not, a `hist()` of a single column would not, an illustration does.

::: {.callout-desc}
**The lesson.** Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of *Exploratory Data Analysis*.
:::
:::

4.4 One variable per facet
Faceting splits the plot into small multiples: one per level of a variable:

    ncol = 1

  theme_dark()









































Different species have different distributions of body mass: a comparison that’s hard to see in one pooled histogram.

text:
4.7 Layers compose
An important ggplot2 habit: plots are built from many layers. For example, scatter + a smooth trend:


ggplot(
    data = penguins, 
    mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)
  ) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.6) + 
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", 
    se = FALSE, 
    color = "#E8A33D", 
    linewidth = 1
  ) + 
  theme_dark()









































geom_point() and geom_smooth() layer on the same plot, each with its own mapping. This layering is what makes ggplot2 so expressive.

text:
1.2 The R ecosystem

R centres on two complementary toolkits:


Base R: ships with every installation, so it needs zero setup (works offline, even in locked-down environments). Functions like mean(), plot(), c(), [. Powerful and always available, but its ergonomics date back decades.


The tidyverse: an opinionated collection of packages (dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, readr) sharing one grammar. Install once, then library(tidyverse) loads them all. The default toolkit for modern data work.


In this course we start from base R so you understand the foundations, then lean on the tidyverse for day-to-day work.

text:
1.3 Alternatives to R
R isn’t the only player. Knowing the landscape helps you choose the right tool.

Stata / SAS / SPSS: proprietary statistical software. Easy for standard methods, certified in regulated settings (health, insurance), but not good programming languages.
Python: a general-purpose language, standard in industry. Not built for statistics, but extremely active in machine learning. More boilerplate for everyday data work; you’ll meet it again in the Reproducible Workflows course.
Julia: a young, fast numerical language. Growing in machine learning, less focused on out-of-the-box data wrangling.
R vs the rest? R gives you the richest statistics ecosystem and the least friction between idea and analysis: at the cost of some “different from other languages” idioms.

title: Foundations: vectors to tables
text:
3.1 Console vs script

Every R statement runs in one of two places:


The Console: type code, see results immediately. Great for quick experiments (2 + 3), inspecting objects (str(x)), and trying one-liners. But what you type is not saved: nothing remains for tomorrow.


An R Script (.R file): your code lives in a file, is persistent, and can be re-run any time (source("my_script.R"), or Cmd/Ctrl+Enter to run the current line). You also get syntax highlighting and autocomplete.


For real work, write in an R script and run it line by line up into the console. The console is for experiments; the script is your reproducible record.


markdown## Console vs script {.paper}

::: {.paper-card}
Every R statement runs in **one of two places**:

::: {.side-panels}
::: {.side-panel .p-console}
**The Console**: type code, see results immediately. Great for quick experiments (`2 + 3`), inspecting objects (`str(x)`), and trying one-liners. But what you type is **not saved**: nothing remains for tomorrow.
:::

::: {.side-panel .p-script}
**An R Script** (`.R` file): your code lives in a file, is **persistent**, and can be re-run any time (`source("my_script.R")`, or Cmd/Ctrl+Enter to run the current line). You also get syntax highlighting and autocomplete.
:::
:::

For real work, **write in an R script** and run it line by line up into the console. The console is for experiments; the script is your reproducible record.

title: Foundations: vectors to tables
text:
3.4 Using functions (1/2)
A function takes arguments and returns a value (just like a mathematical function):


Positional vs named

sqrt(4)        # positional

[1] 2

sqrt(x = 4)    # named

[1] 2










Prefer pkg::function(parameter = argument)


The shortcut function(argument) is risky: two loaded packages can export a same-named function, and dropping parameter names fills arguments by position, so a reordered or missing one fails deep inside the call with a cryptic error. Spelling out package and names keeps calls unambiguous and self-documenting.






Arguments vs parameters. x is the parameter (the name in the function’s definition); 4 is the argument (the value you supply). Some arguments are mandatory, others optional (they have a default value); name the non-obvious ones.


markdown## Using functions (1/2) {.inv}

A **function** takes *arguments* and returns a value (just like a mathematical function):

::: {.split-2}
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Positional vs named
```{r}
sqrt(4)        # positional
sqrt(x = 4)    # named
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Prefer pkg::function(parameter = argument)"}
The shortcut `function(argument)` is risky: two loaded packages can export a same-named function, and dropping parameter names fills arguments by **position**, so a reordered or missing one fails deep inside the call with a cryptic error. Spelling out package and names keeps calls unambiguous and self-documenting.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
**Arguments vs parameters.** `x` is the *parameter* (the name in the function's definition); `4` is the *argument* (the value you supply). Some arguments are **mandatory**, others **optional** (they have a default value); name the non-obvious ones.

text:
3.6 Storing values: assignment



assignment.R

x <- 2         # assign 2 to the name x
x

[1] 2

(x <- 3)       # assign AND print in one go

[1] 3

x <- "Hello"   # now x holds a character string
x

[1] "Hello"













Keyboard shortcut


You can insert <- with:

Alt + - (Windows),
Option + - (Mac).






Use the assignment operator <- to bind a value to an object so you can reuse it later.







<- vs =


You can use = to assign, but don’t: = is also used to set an argument inside a function call, so its meaning depends on context. <- is unambiguous.





markdown## Storing values: assignment {.inv}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="64%"}

3.9 Special values
R has its own vocabulary for edge cases:

NA: missing (“Not Available”). A hole in your data. x <- NA.
NaN: Not a Number, e.g. 0/0. A kind of missing numeric.
Inf: Infinity, e.g. 1/0. Overflow or divergence.
NULL: empty/absent. Means “no value here at all”, different from NA.


Anticipate missingness. NA is contagious: most functions on data containing NA return NA unless you say na.rm = TRUE. We’ll meet this again (and handle it properly) in the data-cleaning lab.


markdown## Special values {.inv}

R has its own vocabulary for edge cases:

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
**[NA]{.green}: missing** ("Not Available"). A hole in your data. `x <- NA`.

**[NaN]{.amber}: Not a Number**, e.g. `0/0`. A *kind* of missing numeric.

**[Inf]{.amber}: Infinity**, e.g. `1/0`. Overflow or divergence.

**[NULL]{.indigo}: empty**/absent. Means "no value here at all", different from `NA`.
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
**Anticipate missingness.** `NA` is contagious: most functions on data containing `NA` return `NA` unless you say `na.rm = TRUE`. We'll meet this again (and handle it properly) in the data-cleaning lab.
:::

Build with c()Sequences

text:
4.5 Subsetting atomic vectors
There are four ways to pick elements with [, grouped into the three kinds below, plus the mental model that unifies them:

PositiveNegativeLogicalCharacterThe key mental model



Positive

x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(3, 2, 5)]   # keep by position

[1] "three" "two"   "five" 






Negative

x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(-1, -3, -5)]   # drop by position, equivalent to

[1] "two"  "four"

x[-c(1, 3, 5)]

[1] "two"  "four"






Logical

x <- c(10, 3, NA, 5, 8, 1, NA)
x[!is.na(x)]

[1] 10  3  5  8  1

x[x %% 2 == 0]

[1] 10 NA  8 NA






Character

x <- c(abc = 1, def = 2, xyz = 5)
x[c("xyz", "def")]

xyz def 
  5   2 





x[selector] returns elements where the selector is TRUE: the logical form.

mental model

x <- c(5, 1, NA, 8, 2)
x[x > 3]        # "x, where x is greater than 3"

[1]  5 NA  8

x[!is.na(x)]    # "x, where x is not missing"

[1] 5 1 8 2




NA trap. x[x %% 2 == 0] keeps NAs too: NA %% 2 == 0 is NA.





markdown## Subsetting atomic vectors {.inv}

There are **four** ways to pick elements with `[`, grouped into the three kinds below, plus the mental model that unifies them:

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Positive
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Positive
```{r}
x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(3, 2, 5)]   # keep by position
```
:::

### Negative
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Negative
```{r}
x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(-1, -3, -5)]   # drop by position, equivalent to
x[-c(1, 3, 5)]
```
:::

### Logical
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Logical
```{r}
x <- c(10, 3, NA, 5, 8, 1, NA)
x[!is.na(x)]
x[x %% 2 == 0]
```
:::

### Character
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Character
```{r}
x <- c(abc = 1, def = 2, xyz = 5)
x[c("xyz", "def")]
```
:::

### The key mental model
`x[selector]` returns elements **where the selector is TRUE**: the **logical** form.

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
mental model
```{r}
x <- c(5, 1, NA, 8, 2)
x[x > 3]        # "x, where x is greater than 3"
x[!is.na(x)]    # "x, where x is not missing"
```
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
**`NA` trap.** `x[x %% 2 == 0]` keeps `NA`s too: `NA %% 2 == 0` is `NA`.
:::
:::

title: Foundations: vectors to tables
text:
4.6 Recycling
When two vectors differ in length, R recycles the shorter one to match the longer:

recycling

c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)

[1] 11 22 13 24




equivalent to

c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20, 10, 20)

[1] 11 22 13 24










Stretch / gotcha


Recycling is powerful but silent; it can zip wrongly-sized vectors together without a warning if the longer length isn’t a multiple. c(1,2,3) == c(1,2) gives TRUE TRUE FALSE with a warning; always sanity-check lengths after mixing.





markdown## Recycling {.inv}

When two vectors differ in length, R **recycles** the shorter one to match the longer:

::: {.codewindow .r width="72%"}
recycling
```{r}
c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)
```
:::

::: {.codewindow .r width="72%"}
equivalent to
```{r}
c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20, 10, 20)
```
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Stretch / gotcha"}
Recycling is powerful but silent; it can zip wrongly-sized vectors together without a warning if the longer length isn't a multiple. `c(1,2,3) == c(1,2)` gives `TRUE TRUE FALSE` with a warning; always sanity-check lengths after mixing.
:::

A list can mix types

text:
5.2 Applying a function to every element
The *apply family does “for each element, run this function”:

lapply / sapply

my_list <- list(var1 = rnorm(n = 20L), var2 = runif(n = 12L), var3 = rbinom(n = 42L, size = 1, prob = 0.5))
lapply(my_list, FUN = mean)   # returns a list

$var1
[1] 0.1767984

$var2
[1] 0.5901083

$var3
[1] 0.5714286

sapply(my_list, FUN = mean)   # tries to simplify to an atomic vector

     var1      var2      var3 
0.1767984 0.5901083 0.5714286 




vapply for safety. vapply(my_list, mean, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1)) promises the output type up front and fails loudly: prefer it in code you ship.


markdown## Applying a function to every element {.inv}

The `*apply` family does "for each element, run this function":

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
`lapply` / `sapply`
```{r}
my_list <- list(var1 = rnorm(n = 20L), var2 = runif(n = 12L), var3 = rbinom(n = 42L, size = 1, prob = 0.5))
lapply(my_list, FUN = mean)   # returns a list
sapply(my_list, FUN = mean)   # tries to simplify to an atomic vector
```
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
**`vapply` for safety.** `vapply(my_list, mean, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1))` promises the output type up front and fails loudly: prefer it in code you ship.
:::

text:
7.1 Working directory & relative paths

Every file path in R is resolved relative to your working directory (the folder R is currently “in”), unless you write an absolute path (/Users/you/...).

getwd()        # where is R right now?
list.files()   # what is in that folder?
setwd("...")   # move elsewhere (avoid in scripts!)









Think in terms of projects


Open your course folder as a project and work there: the working directory is that folder, so a relative path like read_csv("data/raw/penguins.csv") just works. A small, predictable layout keeps things tidy:
my-course/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
└── scripts/
Prefer relative paths; they let a script run on any machine with the same folder layout.





markdown## Working directory & relative paths {.inv}

::: {.split-2}

Every file path in R is resolved **relative to your working directory** (the folder R is currently "in"), unless you write an *absolute* path (`/Users/you/...`).

::: {.codewindow .r width="75%" name="working-directory.R"}
```r
getwd()        # where is R right now?
list.files()   # what is in that folder?
setwd("...")   # move elsewhere (avoid in scripts!)
```
:::

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Think in terms of projects"}
Open your course folder as a **project** and work there: the working directory *is* that folder, so a relative path like `read_csv("data/raw/penguins.csv")` just works. A small, predictable layout keeps things tidy:

```text
my-course/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
└── scripts/
```

Prefer relative paths; they let a script run on any machine with the same folder layout.
:::

Vue d’ensemble des Rencontres R 2026
Les Rencontres R, organisées sous l’égide de la Société Française de Statistique1 (SFdS), ont pour objectif de rassembler une communauté essentiellement francophone (non restrictif) d’utilisateurs du langage de programmation R au sens large. Cela englobe les statistiques, l’analyse de données, l’apprentissage machine, l’intelligence artificielle, le traitement des données, les outils pour la communication, etc., dans toutes les disciplines. R (et l’environnement de travail qu’il représente) est l’un des langages informatiques les plus utilisés pour l’analyse de données issues de toutes les disciplines (sciences du vivant, chimie, physique, médecine, pharmacie, informatique, économie, psychologie, ingénierie, sciences actuarielles, commerce, etc.) aussi bien du secteur public que privé. C’est un logiciel libre, multi-plateforme et gratuit. Son code source est ouvert et une large communauté de développeurs contribue à son essor. En janvier 2025, le site principal de distribution de compléments à R2 comptait plus de 22000 packages. La communauté est constituée aussi bien d’académiques et de scientifiques que d’acteurs issus des secteurs publics et privés et des organisations non gouvernementales.
Les Rencontres R ont débuté à Bordeaux en 2012 et ont lieu, sauf exception, tous les ans. Elles se sont déroulées jusqu’ici dans de grandes villes françaises (Bordeaux 2012, Lyon 2013, Montpellier 2014, Grenoble 2015, Toulouse 2016, Anglet 2017, Rennes 2018, Paris 2021, Avignon 2023 et Vannes 2024) et l’an passé en Belgique (Mons 2025). Il s’agit de la plus grande manifestation francophone de ce genre en Europe. À chaque édition, entre 150 et 220 personnes échangent leurs travaux et points de vue. Les débutants sont bienvenus autant que les utilisateurs chevronnés de R. La communauté se caractérise par une grande ouverture. Après un magnifique congrès à Mons en Belgique l’an passé, pays francophone voisin, Nantes Université, et en particulier le laboratoire de Mathématiques Jean Leray, organise l’édition 2026 sur cinq demi-journées du 16 au 18 juin 2026. Une formation au langage Julia sera probablement organisée au même endroit en amont des Rencontres le 15 juin 2026. Un R Dev Day aura également lieu au même endroit le 19 juin 2026 afin d’offrir la possibilité aux participants de prolonger les échanges dans un cadre plus informel et de découvrir d’autres facettes de l’écosystème R comme celle de contribuer au code source de R ou de ses packages. Dans la lignée des éditions précédentes visant à offrir à la communauté des utilisateurs de R un lieu de rencontre et de partage permettant de développer de nouvelles collaborations, l’édition 2026 accueillera des orateurs nationaux et internationaux invités à partager leur expérience et leur expertise aussi bien auprès d’un public novice qu’expert dans des domaines variés dont la santé, l’environnement, l’archeologie, etc.

Gouvernance des Rencontres R 2026

Comité de pilotage
L’organisation des Rencontres R est guidée par un comité de pilotage (CP). Ce comité a pour rôle de s’assurer que le format de la conférence reste chaque année dans le même esprit que ce qui avait été pensé lors de sa création en 2012. En particulier, le CP veille à ce que les frais d’inscription restent accessibles pour l’ensemble de la communauté, que les personnes impliquées dans l’organisation et le programme soient différentes chaque année en assurant un équilibre académie / industrie & homme / femme, ainsi qu’une diversité des sujets abordés.

Comité d’organisation
Le comité d’organisation (CO) locale prend en charge les différents aspects pratiques du déroulement des Rencontres R, tout en veillant à une continuité dans l’état d’esprit des Rencontres R. Le bon déroulement du colloque se fera aussi grâce au staff du comité de soutien logistique.

Comité scientifique
Le comité scientifique (CS) définit le programme des présentations orales et des communications au format posters. Il garantit l’équilibre et la qualité des interventions par rapport aux différentes thématiques qui constituent ces Rencontres R. Il choisit les conférenciers invités. Il sélectionne les contributions sous forme de communications et de posters. Il établit la liste des sessions et leur déroulement. Il veille, en particulier, à ce que la communauté soit inclusive et balancée, notamment entre participants débutants et plus expérimentés, mais également, en termes de diversité géographique, de genre, d’expérience et de niveau de carrière. Il est composé de membres d’horizons différents (universités et entreprises différentes).

section: Nantes Université, hôte des Rencontres R 2026
text:
Nantes Université, hôte des Rencontres R 2026
Nantes Université (anciennement Université de Nantes jusqu’en 2022) a été créée sous sa forme actuelle en 1961, succédant, presque deux siècles plus tard, à l’université ducale de Bretagne fondée en 1460 à Nantes par François II, duc de Bretagne et dissoute en 1793. La Figure 1 illustre l’université ducale.
Depuis 2022, Nantes Université intègre l’École centrale de Nantes, l’ENSA Nantes et l’école des beaux-arts de Nantes et Saint-Nazaire comme établissements-composantes, et associe à sa gouvernance l’IRT Jules Verne, le CHU de Nantes et l’INSERM. La Figure 2 résume l’organisation actuelle de Nantes Université.









Figure 1: Image du chateau Tertre, symbole de l’université ducale de Bretagne.











Figure 2: Organisation de Nantes Université






Nantes Université est composée de 4 pôles qui regroupent des composantes et des structures de recherche :

Pôle Sociétés (Droit et Sciences politiques, IAE Nantes - Économie et Management, Institut Préparation à l’Administration Générale IPAG, Sociologie)
Pôle Santé (Médecine, Odontologie, Pharmacie, Sciences et techniques des Activités Physiques et Sportives STAPS)
Pôle Humanités (Géographie et Aménagement IGARUN, Histoire-Histoire de l’Art et Archéologie, Langues et Cultures Etrangères FLCE, Lettres et Langage, Psychologie)
Pôles Sciences et Technologie (Polytech’Nantes, IUT de Nantes, IUT de Saint Nazaire, IUT de La Roche-sur-Yon, Sciences et Techniques).

Sur ces 4 pôles se répartissent :











Unités Mixte de Recherche
26














Unités de Recherche
14














Fédérations de Recherche
3














Structure Fédérative de Recherche

Unités d'Appui à la Recherche
