title: Internship Offer
text:
Neuroimaging context

Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) represents 1.5 million hospital admissions in the European Union (EU) each year and approximately 160,000 cases/year in France. Their causes are numerous: accidents, contact sports, military (Bhattrai et al. 2019), etc. It is a leading cause of injury-related death (57,000 TBI-related deaths each year in the EU) and disability, with a devastating impact on patients and their families (Majdan et al. 2016). It is therefore of paramount importance both from a clinical standpoint and from an ethical and societal standpoint to be able to accurately predict functional outcomes. The PASTRAMI project aims to develop a patient-specific prediction model for TBI functional outcomes using neuroimaging data.


Brain microstructure and structural connectivity
The human brain is a complex organ composed of approximately 86 billion neurons and 85 billion non-neuronal cells. The neurons are connected to each other through synapses, which are the key elements of the brain’s information processing system. The brain’s white matter (WM) is composed of axonal bundles that connect different regions of the brain and glial cells that support and protect the neurons. The axonal bundles are organized in a complex network of connections, the so-called connectome. Biological parameters of interest in the context of TBI include axonal density and mean diameter, axonal orientations, glial cell density and mean diameter and proportion of free water. In effect, severe TBI is often associated with axonal injury, which often translates into a decrease in axonal density and mean diameter, and an increase in the proportion of free water.


Diffusion MRI
Diffusion MRI is an imaging modality sensitive to constrained water diffusion in tissues. It is the only non-invasive imaging modality that can provide information about the brain’s microstructure and structural connectivity (Alexander et al. 2019). In particular, using an appropriate model of the diffusion process (Assaf et al. 2004), the above-mentioned biological parameters of interest can be estimated at each voxel of the brain. Once this information is estimated, it can be used, through the process of tractography, to provide a mathematical reconstruction of axonal bundles (Jeurissen et al. 2019). The result of all the preprocessing steps is a set of mathematical objects that jointly represent the brain’s microstructure and structural connectivity. These objects are high-dimensional and complex, and their analysis is a challenging task. In particular, the number of axonal bundles is not known a priori and varies from one individual to another. This makes the comparison of a patient’s brain to healthy brains difficult.

title: Internship Offer
text:
Internship objectives
Mathematically, we define a streamline as an ordered sequence of 3D points \(x_1, \dots, x_M\). Taking the view of functional data analysis, a streamline can be viewed as a parametrized curve \(x(s) \in \mathbb{R}^3\), \(s \in [0,1]\), with \(x(0) = x_1\) and \(x(1) = x_M\). A white matter fascicle is defined as a collection of streamlines connecting to regions of the brain and responsible for the communication between them with the aim of performing a specific function. In addition, at each sampled point of each streamline composing the fascicle, one can add the information about the local microstructure (local tissue composition: number of tissue populations and respective volumes of occupancy, axon density, axon diameter, glial cell diameter, etc.). This information is recovered via diffusion MRI by modeling and estimating constrained diffusion of water in tissue with impermeable membranes and specific geometries (e.g. cylinders or spheres) as a mixture of parametric probability distributions. If we denote by \(\mathcal{M}\) the set of such mixtures of parametrized distributions, we can now define a microstructure-augmented fascicle (MAF) as a collection of parametrized curves \(f_1(s), \dots, f_N(s) \in \mathbb{R}^3
\times \mathcal{M}\), \(s \in [0,1]\), with \(f_i(0) = (x_1^{(i)}, p_1^{(i)})\) and \(f_i(1) = (x_M^{(i)}, p_M^{(i)})\), where \(p_j^{(i)}\) is a mixture of parametric distributions describing diffusion of water (and thus, indirectly, microstructure) locally around the point \(x_j\) on the \(i\)-th streamline.
A MAF of primary importance is the corticospinal tract (CST) sometimes also referred to as the pyramidal tract (PyT), which is the main motor pathway in the human brain. It is responsible for voluntary movement and connects the motor cortex to the spinal cord. The CST is a well-known target for neurosurgical procedures and is often affected in TBI. The method that generates MAFs from diffusion MRI data is called tractography and outputs a number of streamlines that are supposed to represent the fascicle of interest. However, the output of tractography is highly variable and depends on the acquisition protocol, the tractography algorithm, and the post-processing steps. This variability makes it difficult to compare MAFs between patients and healthy controls. The goal of the internship is to develop a statistical model for comparing MAFs between a patient and a healthy population by building a adequate representation of the CST via representative streamlines in such a way that this representation be identifiable across subjects and robust to the variability of tractography.
Care will be taken to ensure that the representation is also interpretable in terms of the underlying microstructure. The candidate will therefore explore the existing literature on Wasserstein barycenters for mixture models (Peyré et al. 2019; Delon and Desolneux 2020) and propose a method to build a representative MAF for the CST. The candidate will also explore the existing literature on the use of functional data analysis (FDA) or topological data analysis (TDA) for:

clustering streamlines: in FDA, we can use the SRF or SRVF representation of the streamlines and apply clustering methods to such data (Kurtek et al. 2012; Srivastava and Klassen 2016). In TDA, we can use the persistence diagrams of the streamlines and apply clustering methods to the persistence diagrams (Chazal and Michel 2021).
comparing the representative MAF to the MAFs of the healthy population which can be framed either as an hypothesis testing problem or as an anomaly detection problem. In both cases, it is of paramount importance not only to tell if there are anomalies but to localize them and to provide a measure of the severity of the anomalies.

The candidate will implement the proposed methods and apply them to a data set of diffusion MRI data from patients with TBI and healthy controls. The candidate will also participate in the writing of a scientific article and the preparation of a presentation of the results.
The internship might be extended to a PhD thesis.

title: phutil 0.0.3
text:
English   French
The goal of the {phutil} package is to provide utility functions for persistence data analysis. In particular, the package defines a data structure for hosting persistence data. The package is part of the TDAverse suite of packages, which aims to provide a consistent interface for topological data analysis in R that nicely integrates with the tidymodels ecosystem.

title: phutil 0.0.3
text:
Installation
You can install the development version of {phutil} from GitHub with:
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("tdaverse/phutil")

title: phutil 0.0.3
text:
The persistence class
The package currently provides a new data structure for hosting persistence data. The data set noisy_circle_points is a simulated data set consisting of 100 points sampled from a circle with additive Gaussian noise using a standard deviation of \(0.05\):


              x          y
[1,]  0.6651721  0.6363172
[2,] -0.7481066 -0.6901262
[3,] -0.8288544 -0.5519689
[4,] -0.7650181 -0.7436499
[5,]  0.6337296 -0.7607464
[6,] -0.6077663 -0.7036492


The data set noisy_circle_ripserr is a persistence diagram computed using the ripserr package with the ripserr::vietoris_rips() and stored as an object of class PHom, which is a light wrapper around a data frame with 3 variables:


  dimension birth       death
1         0     0 0.008162723
2         0     0 0.008548402
3         0     0 0.009238432
4         0     0 0.014004707
5         0     0 0.020555701
6         0     0 0.024621462


The data set noisy_circle_tda_rips is a persistence diagram computed using the TDA package with the TDA::ripsDiag() and stored as a list of length 1 containing the object diagram of class diagram, which is a matrix with 3 columns:


     dimension Birth     Death
[1,]         0     0 1.6322000
[2,]         0     0 0.3677392
[3,]         0     0 0.3325817
[4,]         0     0 0.3226673
[5,]         0     0 0.2096916
[6,]         0     0 0.1953531


The data structure adopted by the TDAverse suite of packages and provided by this package is designed to be a common interface for persistence data. This allows for a seamless integration of persistence data across different packages and ensures that the data is always in a consistent format.
Specifically, the persistence class is a list with the following components:

pairs: A list of 2-column matrices containing birth-death pairs. The -th element of the list corresponds to the -th homology dimension. If there is no pairs for a given dimension but there are pairs in higher dimensions, the corresponding element(s) is/are filled with a numeric matrix.
metadata: A list of length 6 containing information about how the data was computed:

orderered_pairs: A boolean indicating whether the pairs in the pairs list are ordered (i.e. the first column is strictly less than the second column).
data: The name of the object containing the original data on which the persistence data was computed.
engine: The name of the package and the function of this package that computed the persistence data in the form "package_name::package_function".
filtration: The filtration used in the computation in a human-readable format (i.e. full names, capitals where need, etc.).
parameters: A list of parameters used in the computation.
call: The exact call that generated the persistence data.


The as_persistence() function is used to convert persistence data from different packages into the persistence class. For example, the persistence data computed using the ripserr package can be converted into the persistence class as follows:



── Persistence Data ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ℹ There are 99 and 2 pairs in dimensions 0 and 1 respectively.
ℹ Computed from a Vietoris-Rips/Cubical filtration using `ripserr::<vietoris_rips/cubical>()`.
! With unknown parameters.


Similarly, the persistence data computed using the TDA package can be converted into the persistence class as follows:



── Persistence Data ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ℹ There are 100 and 2 pairs in dimensions 0 and 1 respectively.
ℹ Computed from a Vietoris-Rips filtration using `TDA::ripsDiag()`.
ℹ With the following parameters: maxdimension = 1 and maxscale = 1.6322.

title: phutil 0.0.3
text:
Distances between persistence diagrams
The package also provides a function to compute the bottleneck distance between two persistence diagrams. The function bottleneck_distance() takes two persistence diagrams as input and computes the bottleneck distance between them:


[1] 0.06197453


One can also compute the Wasserstein distance between two persistence diagrams using the wasserstein_distance() function:


[1] 1.53403


It is also possible to compute these distances between all pairs of persistence diagrams in a list using e.g. wasserstein_pairwise_distances():


         1        2        3        4
2 1.534030                           
3 2.301812 1.852241                  
4 2.354967 2.362616 1.922799         
5 2.374818 2.707366 1.985518 3.154120


It returns an object of class dist. It is parallelized using OpenMP and relies under the hood on the Hera C++ library which is BSD-licensed. The code interfacing R and C++ is generated by the header-only {cpp11} package which is MIT-licensed.

title: rdatagouv 0.1.0
text:
English   French
rdatagouv is an R client for the public API of data.gouv.fr, the French government’s open data platform. It helps you find a dataset that matches your interests, judge whether it is usable, download it, and later re-fetch the exact same table reproducibly. Requests are built on top of the httr2 package.

text:
Installation

# install.packages("pak") # if you don't have pak yet
pak::pak("rdatagouv")
Alternatively, you can install the development version from GitHub:
pak::pak("astamm/rdatagouv")

title: rdatagouv 0.1.0

  gt::gt() |>

    quality_score = "Quality Score"

title: rdatagouv 0.1.0
text:
Supported formats
dg_pull_dataset() downloads the first tabular resource of a dataset among CSV, CSV.GZ, XLS, XLSX, PARQUET, TSV, TXT and JSON, and returns the parsed table as a single tibble. A ZIP resource is unpacked and its first parseable file is returned by default; all_files = TRUE keeps every contained file in one of these formats as a named list — one element per file. The delimiter of CSV/TXT resources is auto-detected (comma, semicolon, tab, pipe, …), so both standard and European-style (semicolon/comma-decimal) files are handled without special configuration. Column types are inferred by vroom, but seeded by default from data.gouv’s own csv-detective profile (use_tabular_types = TRUE) and you can force specific columns with col_types = c(col = "Date") (e.g. to make a mostly-padded ISO date column with a few non-padded stragglers read as Date, turning the stragglers into NA; explicit col_types always win). The profile is a best-effort signal — it only exists for single-file resources indexed by the tabular service, and a missing profile (or a ZIP member) falls back to type inference; pass use_tabular_types = FALSE to disable seeding entirely. Any parsing issues are attached to the returned table as an rdatagouv_problems attribute — read them with dg_problems(tbl) — rather than a noisy per-cell warning.
The discovery catalog (dg_find_datasets()) is restricted to the official tabular formats data.gouv.fr itself indexes (csv, csv.gz, xls, xlsx, parquet), so every listed dataset is in principle openable as a table. Use the format argument to narrow the catalog to datasets with a resource in a specific format (the v2 search API matches several formats as a server-side union). The exact n_resources/formats/has_table/has_schema resource columns are populated by passing resources = TRUE. Direct pulls additionally accept tsv, txt and json resources.

title: New paper on domain selection for functional data
text:
English   French Functional data are smooth, often continuous, random curves, which can be seen as an extreme case of multivariate data with infinite dimensionality. Just as component-wise inference for multivariate data naturally performs feature selection, subset-wise inference for functional data performs domain selection. In this paper, we present a unified testing framework for domain selection on populations of functional data. In detail, \(p\)-values of hypothesis tests performed on point-wise evaluations of functional data are suitably adjusted for providing control of the family-wise error rate (FWER) over a family of subsets of the domain. We show that several state-of-the-art domain selection methods fit within this framework and differ from each other by the choice of the family over which the control of the FWER is provided. In the existing literature, these families are always defined a priori. In this work, we also propose a novel approach, coined threshold-wise testing, in which the family of subsets is instead built in a data-driven fashion. The method seamlessly generalizes to multidimensional domains in contrast to methods based on a priori defined families. We provide theoretical results with respect to consistency and control of the FWER for the methods within the unified framework. We illustrate the performance of the methods within the unified framework on simulated and real data examples and compare their performance with other existing methods.
Find out more by reading our paper (Abramowicz et al. 2022) which can be found at https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/biom.13669.




References

Abramowicz, Konrad, Alessia Pini, Lina Schelin, Sara Sjöstedt de Luna, Aymeric Stamm, and Simone Vantini. 2022. “Domain Selection and Family-Wise Error Rate for Functional Data: A Unified Framework.” Biometrics, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.13669.

title: nloptr 2.0.0
text:
nlopt
The NLopt library (Johnson 2021) is a free/open-source library for nonlinear optimization, providing a common interface for a number of different free optimization routines available online as well as original implementations of various other algorithms.
Starting from v2.5.0, NLopt has switched to cmake as build system, making the latest versions incompatible with the way nloptr used to interface the library.

title: nloptr 2.0.0
text:
nloptr
As of v2.0.0, we now provide an R interface to nlopt >= 2.7.0. This is achieved in different ways depending on the operating system you are using.

Windows
There is no dependency required for Windows users.

If you are running on R <= 4.1.x, installation of nloptr will rely on a valid internet connexion to download the nlopt 2.7.1 headers and static library from rwinlib and use it.
If you are running on R >= 4.2.x, installation of nloptr will directly link with nlopt 2.7.1 from the Rtools42 toolchain.



Linux and macOS
On Unix-like systems, installation of nloptr will go through the following steps:
Is pkg-config available on your PATH?

NO: compile nlopt 2.7.1 from included sources using cmake >= 3.15.0.
YES: can pkg-config detect a system build of nlopt >= 2.7.0?

NO: compile nlopt 2.7.1 from included sources using cmake >= 3.15.0.
YES: install nloptr using the detected system build of nlopt.


Hence, cmake >= 3.15.0 can become a system requirement for installing nloptr on your machine if you are running on a Unix-like system without pkg-config or without a system build of nlopt >= 2.7.0.

title: squat 0.3.0
text: English   French

title: squat 0.3.0
text:
Overview
The goal of squat is to provide extensions of common statistical methods for the analysis of rotation-valued time series and functional data. Three-dimensional rotations can be represented in at least five different ways:

\(3\times 3\) symmetric definite positive matrices with unit determinant;
pair of axis (3D unit vector) and angle (real) of rotation;
Euler angles;
Tait-Bryan angles;
Unit quaternions.

This package mainly focuses on methods in which rotations are represented via unit quaternions. To this end, it exploits the excellent API for quaternions available as part of the Eigen library.
The package is currently structured into 8 sections:

New class for QTS. A collection of functions that define the [qts] class for storing quaterion time series (QTS). It provides tools for centering and standardizing a single QTS and for visualizing a single QTS.
New class for QTS sample. A collection of functions that define the [qts_sample] class for storing samples of QTS. It provides tools to (i) randomly sample QTS with Gaussian noise on the QTS logarithm, (ii) center and standarize samples, (iii) compute the mean or median and (iv) visualize samples of QTS.
QTS Wrangling. A collection of functions to manipulate QTS: differentiation, straightening, logarithm and exponential maps, reorientation, normalization, resampling, smoothing, hemispherization, moving average.
Transformations of QTS. A collection of functions to transform QTS into real-valued time series: (i) distance time series (pointwise geodesic distance between two input QTS at each time point), norm time series, angle time series (angle between the first and other attitudes at each time point) and angular velocity time series.
Principal Component Analysis. An S3 specialization of the prcomp() method for QTS samples with visualization tools. It performs PCA in the Lie algebra of the 3-sphere.
Clustering. A collection of functions to perform clustering of a sample of QTS. It includes (i) an S3 specialization of the kmeans() method for QTS samples, (ii) an S3 specialization of the hclust() method for QTS samples and (iii) an S3 specialization of the dbscan() method for QTS samples. All clustering algorithms return an object of class qtsclust which can be visualized via S3 specializations of the ggplot2::autoplot() and plot() methods.
Distance matrix computation. An S3 specialization of the dist() method for computing a pairwise distance matrix from a QTS sample using either the \(L^2\) distance or a Pearson-based distance or the dynamic time warping metric from time series analysis.
Data sets. Two datasets for illustrations, examples and case studies.

title: midi 0.1.0
text: English   French

title: midi 0.1.0
text:
Overview
The Human brain can be seen as grey matter and white matter. The former is composed of cell bodies and dendrites, while the latter is composed of axons and glial cells. Neurons are made up of a cell body, dendrites, and an axon. The cell body contains the nucleus and other organelles, and the dendrites receive electrical signals from other neurons. The axon is a long, thin projection that carries signals away from the cell body to other neurons. The axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath, which is a fatty substance that insulates the axons and speeds up the transmission of electrical signals. The myelin sheath is not continuous, but rather has small gaps called nodes of Ranvier. The axons are bundled together in what is called a fiber bundle. The glial cells are responsible for maintaining the homeostasis of the brain and providing support and protection for the axons.
The scale of these tissues (of the order of micrometers) makes them invisible to the naked eye. However, a robust reconstruction of the brain microstructure is key to understanding brain function and dysfunction. This is where diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) comes in. Water molcules are in constant random motion due to their thermal energy and our body is made of 80% of water. The diffusion of water molecules in the brain is restricted by the cell membranes and myelin sheaths, and is faster along the axons than perpendicular to them. This anisotropic diffusion can be measured using diffusion MRI. Diffusion MRI is a non-invasive imaging technique which makes the magnetization of protons sensitive to the diffusion by applying so-called magnetic field diffusion gradients. The signal attenuation in diffusion MRI is then used to infer the microstructure of the brain.
An enormous amount of research has been done to understand the relationship between the signal attenuation and the microstructure of the brain and many parametric models have been devised to describe this relationship. However, the spatial resolution of diffusion MRI is limited by the voxel size, which is typically in the order of millimeters, therefore containing many different tissue types. In addition, depending on the experimental conditions (number, duration and strength of the gradients and time between two consecutive gradients), the MR signal might not be sensitive to all tissue types in the voxel. The midi package is meant to list the tissue models that have been proposed in the literature and to provide tools to simulate the MR signal attenuation predicted by these models under different experimental conditions.
The package is then used in an eponymous Shiny web application which provides a user-friendly interface for the package and allows to interactively visualize the MR signal attenuation induced by the different tissue models and design experimental conditions to optimize the sensitivity to specific tissue parameters. The Shiny web application can be launched with the midi::run_app() function for convenience but can be directly accessed at the following URL: https://midi-pastrami.apps.math.cnrs.fr/.
The package has its own webpage: https://lmjl-alea.github.io/midi/.

title: midi 0.1.0
text:
Installation
You can install the released version of midi from CRAN with:
install.packages("midi")
You can install the development version of midi from GitHub with:
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("lmjl-alea/midi")

title: midi 0.1.0
text:
Example
We can instantiate a cylinder bundle compartment as follows:

library(midi)
cylinderComp <- CylinderCompartment$new(
  axis = c(0, 0, 1),
  restricted_compartment = VanGelderenCompartment$new(
    radius = 1e-5,
    diffusivity = 2.0e-9
  )
)
cylinderBundleComp <- CylinderBundleCompartment$new(
  cylinder_density = 0.5,
  cylinder_compartments = list(cylinderComp)
)

Note that the instantiation of the compartment requires the specification of the cylinder axis, radius, diffusivity, cylinder density, and radial model, which are only the parameters related to the cylinder bundle geometry.
The parameters related to the experimental conditions are specified when calling the get_signal method which computes the signal attenuation for the compartment. In this example, we consider the following experimental conditions:

cylinderBundleComp$get_signal(
  small_delta = 0.03,
  big_delta = 0.03,
  G = 0.040,
  direction = c(0, 0, 1)
)

[1] 1


We can also simulate and visualize cylinder bundles:

density <- 0.7
voxel_size <- 5 # micrometers

title: squat 0.2.0
text:
Overview
The goal of squat is to provide extensions of common statistical methods for the analysis of rotation-valued time series and functional data. Three-dimensional rotations can be represented in at least five different ways:

\(3\times 3\) symmetric definite positive matrices with unit determinant;
pair of axis (3D unit vector) and angle (real) of rotation;
Euler angles;
Tait-Bryan angles;
Unit quaternions.

This package mainly focuses on methods in which rotations are represented via unit quaternions. To this end, it exploits the excellent API for quaternions available as part of the Eigen library.
The package is currently structured into 8 sections:

New class for QTS. A collection of functions that define the [qts] class for storing quaterion time series (QTS). It provides tools for centering and standardizing a single QTS and for visualizing a single QTS.
New class for QTS sample. A collection of functions that define the [qts_sample] class for storing samples of QTS. It provides tools to (i) randomly sample QTS with Gaussian noise on the QTS logarithm, (ii) center and standarize samples, (iii) compute the mean or median and (iv) visualize samples of QTS.
QTS Wrangling. A collection of functions to manipulate QTS: differentiation, straightening, logarithm and exponential maps, reorientation, normalization, resampling, smoothing, hemispherization, moving average.
Transformations of QTS. A collection of functions to transform QTS into real-valued time series: (i) distance time series (pointwise geodesic distance between two input QTS at each time point), norm time series, angle time series (angle between the first and other attitudes at each time point) and angular velocity time series.
Principal Component Analysis. An S3 specialization of the prcomp() method for QTS samples with visualization tools. It performs PCA in the Lie algebra of the 3-sphere.
Clustering. A collection of functions to perform clustering of a sample of QTS. It includes (i) an S3 specialization of the kmeans() method for QTS samples, (ii) an S3 specialization of the hclust() method for QTS samples and (iii) an S3 specialization of the dbscan() method for QTS samples. All clustering algorithms return an object of class qtsclust which can be visualized via S3 specializations of the ggplot2::autoplot() and plot() methods.
Distance matrix computation. An S3 specialization of the dist() method for computing a pairwise distance matrix from a QTS sample using either the \(L^2\) distance or a Pearson-based distance or the dynamic time warping metric from time series analysis.
Data sets. Two datasets for illustrations, examples and case studies.

title: New paper on smoothing methods for rotation-valued functional data
text:
English   French Smoothing orientation data is a fundamental task in different fields of research. Different methods of smoothing time series in quaternion algebras have been described in the literature, but their application is still an open point. This paper develops a smoothing approach for smoothing quaternion time series to obtain good performance in classification problems. Starting from an existing method which involves an angular velocity transformation of unit quaternion time series, a new method which employ the logarithm function to transform the quaternion time series to a real three-dimensional time series is proposed. Empirical evidences achieved on real data set and artificially noisy data sets confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method compared with the classical approach based on angular velocity transformation. The R functions developed for this paper will be provided in a Github repository.
Find out more by reading our paper (Ballante et al. 2023) which can be found at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-36480-y.




References

Ballante, Elena, Lise Bellanger, Pierre Drouin, Silvia Figini, and Aymeric Stamm. 2023. “Smoothing Method for Unit Quaternion Time Series in a Classification Problem: An Application to Motion Data.” Scientific Reports 13 (1): 9366. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-36480-y.

title: nevada 0.1.0
text:
Summary
The package nevada (NEtwork-VAlued Data Analysis) is an R package for the statistical analysis of network-valued data. In this setting, a sample is made of statistical units that are networks themselves. The package provides a set of matrix representations for networks so that network-valued data can be transformed into matrix-valued data. Subsequently, a number of distances between matrices is provided as well to quantify how far two networks are from each other and several test statistics are proposed for testing equality in distribution between samples of networks using exact permutation testing procedures. The permutation scheme is carried out by the flipr package which also provides a number of test statistics based on inter-point distances that play nicely with network-valued data. The implementation is largely made in C++ and the matrix of inter- and intra-sample distances is pre-computed, which alleviates the computational burden often associated with permutation tests.

title: nevada 0.1.0
text:
Pipeline
Network-valued data are data in which the statistical unit is a network itself. This is the data with which we can make inference on populations of networks from samples of networks. The nevada package proposes a specific nvd class to handle network-valued data. Inference from such samples is made possible though a 4-step procedure:

Choose a suitable representation of your samples of networks.
Choose a suitable distance to embed your representation into a nice metric space.
Choose one or more test statistics to define your alternative hypothesis.
Compute an empirical permutation-based approximation of the null distribution.

The package focuses for now on the two-sample testing problem and assumes that all networks from both samples share the same node structure.
There are two types of questions that one can ask:

Is there a difference between the distributions that generated the two observed samples?
Can we localize the differences between the distributions on the node structure?

The nevada package offers a dedicated function for answering each of these two questions:

test2_global(); for more details, please see Lovato et al. (2020),
test2_local(); for more details, please see Lovato et al. (2021).

title: midi 0.2.0
text:
Overview
The Human brain can be seen as grey matter and white matter. The former is composed of cell bodies and dendrites, while the latter is composed of axons and glial cells. Neurons are made up of a cell body, dendrites, and an axon. The cell body contains the nucleus and other organelles, and the dendrites receive electrical signals from other neurons. The axon is a long, thin projection that carries signals away from the cell body to other neurons. The axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath, which is a fatty substance that insulates the axons and speeds up the transmission of electrical signals. The myelin sheath is not continuous, but rather has small gaps called nodes of Ranvier. The axons are bundled together in what is called a fiber bundle. The glial cells are responsible for maintaining the homeostasis of the brain and providing support and protection for the axons.
The scale of these tissues (of the order of micrometers) makes them invisible to the naked eye. However, a robust reconstruction of the brain microstructure is key to understanding brain function and dysfunction. This is where diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) comes in. Water molcules are in constant random motion due to their thermal energy and our body is made of 80% of water. The diffusion of water molecules in the brain is restricted by the cell membranes and myelin sheaths, and is faster along the axons than perpendicular to them. This anisotropic diffusion can be measured using diffusion MRI. Diffusion MRI is a non-invasive imaging technique which makes the magnetization of protons sensitive to the diffusion by applying so-called magnetic field diffusion gradients. The signal attenuation in diffusion MRI is then used to infer the microstructure of the brain.
An enormous amount of research has been done to understand the relationship between the signal attenuation and the microstructure of the brain and many parametric models have been devised to describe this relationship. However, the spatial resolution of diffusion MRI is limited by the voxel size, which is typically in the order of millimeters, therefore containing many different tissue types. In addition, depending on the experimental conditions (number, duration and strength of the gradients and time between two consecutive gradients), the MR signal might not be sensitive to all tissue types in the voxel. The midi package is meant to list the tissue models that have been proposed in the literature and to provide tools to simulate the MR signal attenuation predicted by these models under different experimental conditions.
The package is then used in an eponymous Shiny web application which provides a user-friendly interface for the package and allows to interactively visualize the MR signal attenuation induced by the different tissue models and design experimental conditions to optimize the sensitivity to specific tissue parameters. The Shiny web application can be launched with the midi::run_app() function for convenience but can be directly accessed at the following URL: https://midi-pastrami.apps.math.cnrs.fr/.
The package has its own webpage: https://lmjl-alea.github.io/midi/.

title: midi 0.2.0
text:
Example
We can instantiate a cylinder bundle compartment as follows:

library(midi)
cylinderComp <- CylinderCompartment$new(
  axis = c(0, 0, 1),
  restricted_compartment = VanGelderenCompartment$new(
    radius = 1e-5,
    diffusivity = 2.0e-9
  )
)
cylinderBundleComp <- CylinderBundleCompartment$new(
  cylinder_density = 0.5,
  cylinder_compartments = list(cylinderComp)
)

Note that the instantiation of the compartment requires the specification of the cylinder axis, radius, diffusivity, cylinder density, and radial model, which are only the parameters related to the cylinder bundle geometry.
The parameters related to the experimental conditions are specified when calling the get_signal method which computes the signal attenuation for the compartment. In this example, we consider the following experimental conditions:

cylinderBundleComp$get_signal(
  small_delta = 0.03,
  big_delta = 0.03,
  G = 0.040,
  direction = c(0, 0, 1)
)

[1] 1


We can also simulate and visualize cylinder bundles:

density <- 0.7
voxel_size <- 5 # micrometers
out <- simulate_bundle(density, voxel_size)
plot(out)








A 3D visualization of the cylinder bundle powered by the plotly package can be obtained by calling plot3d():

plot3d(out)

title: midi 0.2.0
text:
News in v0.2.0

Breaking changes

The unit system has changed from SI units (m, s, T/m) to μm, ms, and μT/μm throughout all compartment classes and helper functions.
CylinderBundleCompartment$new() no longer accepts axis, radius, diffusivity, n_cylinders, axis_concentration, radius_sd, radial_model, and seed arguments. It now accepts cylinder_compartments, a list of CylinderCompartment objects (typically produced by rcylinders()), and infers axis, radius, and diffusivity statistics by fitting Watson and Gamma distributions to the provided compartments.
CylinderCompartment$new() no longer accepts radius, diffusivity, and radial_model arguments. It now accepts a restricted_compartment argument, an instance of a circularly-shaped compartment class (e.g., VanGelderenCompartment$new()).



New features

New bvalue() function to compute the b-value from gradient pulse parameters.
New FreeCompartment class to model free unconstrained diffusion.
New GammaDistribution class providing fit(), random(), get_mean(), get_variance(), get_shape(), and get_scale() methods.
New rcylinders() function to sample a list of CylinderCompartment objects from Watson (axis) and Gamma (radius, diffusivity) distributions.
New SphereCompartment class to model restricted diffusion in a sphere.
New WatsonDistribution class providing fit(), random(), get_axis(), and get_concentration() methods.
All compartment classes now expose get_parameters() and get_parameter_names() methods inherited from the new BaseCompartment base class.

title: riot 0.0.1
text:
Overview
The riot (R Input/Output for Tractography) package provides an R interface for importing and exporting tractography data to and from R. Currently supported importing formats are:

native VTK .vtk and .vtp files; and,
medInria `.fds’ files.

The package reads tractography data into a tibble in which each row is a point characterized by at least the following five variables:

X, Y, Z: 3D coordinates of the current point;
PointId: Identification number of the current point among all points of the streamline it belongs to;
StreamlineId: Identification number of the streamline which the current point belongs to.

The points might also have attributes or a color assigned to them, in which case, additional variables will be properly created to import them as well. The user can perform statistical analysis on the point cloud and store any new variable that (s)he would deem to be useful as additional column of the tibble. The packages also allow to write back the tibble, including all newly created attributes, into the following exporting formats:

native VTK .vtk and .vtp files; or,
medInria .fds files.

text:
2.2 for loops
Repeat a block a fixed number of times: the body runs once per value:



for (i in 1:5) {
  # i takes each value of the sequence in turn
  print(i^2)
}


[1] 1
[1] 4
[1] 9
[1] 16
[1] 25




total <- 0
for (x in c(2, 4, 6, 8)) {
  # the body runs once per value
  total <- total + x
}
total


[1] 20




Afterwards i and x are normal variables: they still hold the loop’s last value.


markdown## `for` loops {.inv}

Repeat a block a fixed number of times: the body runs once per value:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="01-for-loops.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
for (i in 1:5) {
  # i takes each value of the sequence in turn
  print(i^2)
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
total <- 0
for (x in c(2, 4, 6, 8)) {
  # the body runs once per value
  total <- total + x
}
total
```
:::

::: {.paper-card}
Afterwards `i` and `x` are normal variables: they still hold the loop's last value.
:::

title: Repeat & package: loops, matrices, functions
text:
2.3 Pre-allocate for speed
Growing a vector inside a loop is slow. Pre-allocate the result first:



n <- 1000L
# a numeric vector of n zeros
out <- numeric(length = n) 
# character(length = n): character vector with n ""
# logical(length = n): logical vector with n FALSE
# integer(length = n): integer vector with n 0L 
# vector(mode = "list", length = n): list with n NULL
for (i in 1:n) {
  out[i] <- rnorm(1)
}
par(bg = "white")
hist(out)











Rule of thumb. Decide the output’s length before the loop, create the container, then fill slots by index (out[i] <- ...). This is much faster than out <- c(out, ...) inside the loop, a habit that matters once your data grows.


markdown## Pre-allocate for speed {.inv}

Growing a vector inside a loop is slow. **Pre-allocate** the result first:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="02-preallocate.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
n <- 1000L
# a numeric vector of n zeros
out <- numeric(length = n) 
# character(length = n): character vector with n ""
# logical(length = n): logical vector with n FALSE
# integer(length = n): integer vector with n 0L 
# vector(mode = "list", length = n): list with n NULL
for (i in 1:n) {
  out[i] <- rnorm(1)
}
par(bg = "white")
hist(out)
```
:::

::: {.paper-card}
**Rule of thumb.** Decide the output's length *before* the loop, create the container, then fill slots by index (`out[i] <- ...`). This is much faster than `out <- c(out, ...)` inside the loop, a habit that matters once your data grows.
:::

title: Repeat & package: loops, matrices, functions
text:
2.4 while loops
Repeat while a condition holds: useful when you don’t know the number of steps in advance:



x <- 1
while (x < 1000) {
  x <- x * 2
}
x


[1] 1024










Guard against infinite loops


If the condition never becomes FALSE, the loop runs forever. Always add a safeguard, e.g.:
x <- 1
max_iter <- 10
counter <- 0
while (x < 1000 && counter < max_iter) {
  x <- x * 2
  counter <- counter + 1
}





markdown## `while` loops {.inv}

Repeat *while a condition holds*: useful when you don't know the number of steps in advance:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="03-while-loops.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
x <- 1
while (x < 1000) {
  x <- x * 2
}
x
```
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Guard against infinite loops"}
If the condition never becomes `FALSE`, the loop runs forever. Always add a safeguard, e.g.:

```r
x <- 1
max_iter <- 10
counter <- 0
while (x < 1000 && counter < max_iter) {
  x <- x * 2
  counter <- counter + 1
}
```

:::

text:
2.6 Element-wise choice: ifelse
For vectorised decisions, use ifelse(condition, when_true, when_false):



temps <- c(-2, 15, 28, 33)
ifelse(temps > 25, "hot", "not hot")


[1] "not hot" "not hot" "hot"     "hot"    



It applies the branch element-wise to a whole vector: no loop needed. This is the idiomatic replacement for “for each value, choose one of two things”.

if vs ifelse.

Use if/else to choose which block of code runs once;
Use ifelse to map a vector to one of two values.

Mixing them up is a classic beginner bug.


markdown## Element-wise choice: `ifelse` {.inv}

For **vectorised** decisions, use `ifelse(condition, when_true, when_false)`:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="05-ifelse.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
temps <- c(-2, 15, 28, 33)
ifelse(temps > 25, "hot", "not hot")
```
:::

It applies the branch *element-wise* to a whole vector: no loop needed. This is the idiomatic replacement for "for each value, choose one of two things".

::: {.paper-card}
**`if` vs `ifelse`.**

- Use `if/else` to choose *which block of code* runs once;
- Use `ifelse` to map a *vector* to one of two values.

Mixing them up is a classic beginner bug.
:::

title: Repeat & package: loops, matrices, functions
text:
2.7 Which tool when?

for: repeat a block a known number of times (loop over columns, pre-allocated slots).
while: repeat until a condition flips (unknown count of steps).
if/else: choose one block of code based on a condition.
ifelse: map a vector element-wise to one of two values.
*apply family: apply a function to each element (Session 1 lists, matrices below).

Often the cleanest loop is no loop at all: vectorization, ifelse, or lapply/vapply are simpler than an explicit for.



markdown## Which tool when? {.inv}

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
**`for`**: repeat a block a *known* number of times (loop over columns, pre-allocated slots).

**`while`**: repeat *until a condition* flips (unknown count of steps).

**`if/else`**: choose *one block of code* based on a condition.

**`ifelse`**: map a *vector* element-wise to one of two values.

**`*apply` family**: apply a function to each element (Session 1 lists, matrices below).

::: {.paper-card}
Often the *cleanest* loop is no loop at all: vectorization, `ifelse`, or `lapply`/`vapply` are simpler than an explicit `for`.
:::

:::

title: Repeat & package: loops, matrices, functions
text:
2.8 The *apply family: loop & apply
Say “apply this function to every element” instead of writing the loop by hand:



l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
lapply(l, mean)          # a list back — keeps the original structure

$a
[1] 2

$b
[1] 5





l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
sapply(l, mean)          # tries to simplify: a named vector

a b 
2 5 





l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
vapply(l, mean, 0)       # like sapply, but you promise the output type

a b 
2 5 





The family you first met on lists in Session 1 (and will meet again on matrices as apply, MARGIN = ...):

lapply always,
sapply when simple,
vapply when you want the guarantee.

It’s “loop, then apply” collapsed into one verb.


markdown## The `*apply` family: loop & apply {.inv}

Say "**apply this function to every element**" instead of writing the loop by hand:

::: {.codewindow}

::: {.editor .r name="lapply.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
lapply(l, mean)          # a list back — keeps the original structure
```
:::

::: {.editor .r .fragment name="sapply.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
sapply(l, mean)          # tries to simplify: a named vector
```
:::

::: {.editor .r .fragment name="vapply.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
vapply(l, mean, 0)       # like sapply, but you promise the output type
```
:::

:::

::: {.paper-card .fragment fragment-index=3}
The family you first met on lists in **Session 1** (and will meet again on matrices as `apply`, `MARGIN = ...`):

- `lapply` always,
- `sapply` when simple,
- `vapply` when you want the guarantee.

It's "loop, *then* apply" collapsed into one verb.

3.1 What is a matrix?
A matrix is a two-dimensional rectangular array of one type (usually numeric): a vector folded into rows and columns. It’s the 2D cousin of the vector.

dim(m) # length-2 vector with dimensions

nrow(m) # number of rows


[1] 3




ncol(m) # number of columns


[1] 4




Key distinction. A data frame is a list of columns (columns may differ in type); a matrix is one vector in 2D (single type). For tabular data with mixed types, prefer a data frame/tibble; reach for a matrix when you need linear algebra.


markdown## What is a matrix? {.inv}

A **matrix** is a *two-dimensional rectangular array* of **one type** (usually numeric): a vector folded into rows and columns. It's the **2D cousin of the vector**.

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="matrix.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
(m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4))
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
m[2, ] # subset with [row, col], like a data frame
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
dim(m) # length-2 vector with dimensions
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
nrow(m) # number of rows
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
ncol(m) # number of columns
```
:::

::: {.paper-card}
**Key distinction.** A data frame is a *list of columns* (columns may differ in type); a matrix is *one vector in 2D* (single type). For tabular *data* with mixed types, prefer a data frame/tibble; reach for a matrix when you need **linear algebra**.
:::

text:
3.2 Building & reshaping
A matrix is just a vector with a dim(ension) attribute; you can build or reshape them freely:



# column-major fill
(A <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3))


     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6




# rbind: bind by row
identical(A, rbind(1:3, 4:6))


[1] FALSE




# cbind: bind by column
cbind(A, c(7, 8))


     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    3    5    7
[2,]    2    4    6    8




# strip the dim -> back to a vector
dim(A) <- NULL 
A


[1] 1 2 3 4 5 6










Column-major by default


matrix() fills column by column unless you pass byrow = TRUE. A classic source of “why is my matrix transposed?” surprises.

text:
3.3 Arithmetic & recycling
Element-wise arithmetic works like it does on vectors, and recycling applies:



(M <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3))


     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6




# scalar multiplies every entry
M * 2


     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    2    6   10
[2,]    4    8   12




# length-2 vector recycles down the COLUMNS
M + c(10, 20)


     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   11   13   15
[2,]   22   24   26




Watch the recycling axis. A length-2 vector recycles along columns (down), not across: get this wrong and your standardisation silently miscalculates each column.

text:
3.4 Linear algebra
Matrices exist to do algebra: matrix product, transpose, inverse, determinant:




(A <- matrix(c(2, 4, 1, 3), nrow = 2))


     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    2    1
[2,]    4    3




A %*% t(A) # matrix product


     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    5   11
[2,]   11   25




t(A) # transpose


     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    2    4
[2,]    1    3






solve(A) # inverse


     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  1.5 -0.5
[2,] -2.0  1.0




(A <- matrix(c(2, 4, 1, 3), nrow = 2))


     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    2    1
[2,]    4    3




det(A) # determinant


[1] 2




diag(A) # extract diagonal


[1] 2 3






eigen(A) # eigen decomposition


eigen() decomposition
$values
[1] 4.5615528 0.4384472

$vectors
           [,1]       [,2]
[1,] -0.3636591 -0.5392856
[2,] -0.9315321  0.8421229











%*% is not *



A * B is element-wise;
A %*% B is the matrix product (rows × columns).

Absent the right dimensions, %*% errors, which is usually the clue you wanted a matrix, not a data frame.

nums <- iris[, 1:4] # 150 x 4, all numeric

text:
3.6 Row/column summaries & apply
Summarise along one axis with the row*/col* helpers, or generalise with apply:



(M <- matrix(1:12, 3, 4))


     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    4    7   10
[2,]    2    5    8   11
[3,]    3    6    9   12




# per row (MARGIN = 1) - see also rowSums(M)
rowMeans(M)


[1] 5.5 6.5 7.5




# per column (MARGIN = 2) - see also colSums(M)
colMeans(M)


[1]  2  5  8 11




# standard deviation of each row
apply(M, 1, sd)


[1] 3.872983 3.872983 3.872983




# range of each column

[1] 2 2 2 2




apply(M, MARGIN, fun): MARGIN = 1 goes down rows, MARGIN = 2 across columns. It’s lapply’s 2D sibling: a loop over one axis hidden inside a one-liner.

title: Repeat & package: loops, matrices, functions
text:
3.7 Standardise a matrix (full example)
Let’s standardize (z-score) every column of a matrix, the machinery behind a real analysis:


M   <- matrix(c(1, 100, 2, 200), 2, 2)
mu  <- colMeans(M)            # mean of each column
sig <- apply(M, 2, sd)        # sd of each column
Z   <- sweep(M, 2, mu,  "-")  # subtract each column's mean
Z   <- sweep(Z, 2, sig, "/")  # divide each column's sd



colMeans(Z)                   # ~ 0


[1] 0 0




apply(Z, 2, sd)               # ~ 1


[1] 1 1




sweep(M, MARGIN, vector, FUN) applies a function across one axis, here subtracting a column mean.
This is the pattern scale(M) automates; you now see what’s underneath.


markdown## Standardise a matrix (full example) {.inv}

Let's **standardize** (z-score) every column of a matrix, the machinery behind a real analysis:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="scale.R"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
M   <- matrix(c(1, 100, 2, 200), 2, 2)
mu  <- colMeans(M)            # mean of each column
sig <- apply(M, 2, sd)        # sd of each column
Z   <- sweep(M, 2, mu,  "-")  # subtract each column's mean
Z   <- sweep(Z, 2, sig, "/")  # divide each column's sd
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
colMeans(Z)                   # ~ 0
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
apply(Z, 2, sd)               # ~ 1
```
:::

::: {.paper-card}
`sweep(M, MARGIN, vector, FUN)` applies a function across one axis, here subtracting a column mean.

This is the pattern `scale(M)` automates; you now see what's underneath.
:::

section: 4.6 When functions aren’t vectorised: Vectorize() & replicate()
text:
4.6 When functions aren’t vectorised: Vectorize() & replicate()
Built-in functions are usually vectorised, but your own (or a third-party) function may only accept one scalar at a time. Two loop-free helpers:


# not vectorised: takes one date string
parse_it <- function(x) strsplit(x, "-")[[1]][1]



# only the first is parsed
parse_it(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))


[1] "2024"




# wraps it => element-wise
parse_all <- Vectorize(parse_it)
parse_all(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))


2024-05-01 2024-06-15 
    "2024"     "2024" 




# repeat an expression R times
replicate(4, mean(rexp(10)))


[1] 1.1850736 0.5272292 0.8328731 0.8861594




Loops without loops. Vectorize() turns a scalar-only function into a vector one; replicate(R, expr) re-runs an expression R times and collects results, the function-flavoured cousin of for/sapply. Works with any expression, not just a named function.


markdown## When functions aren't vectorised: `Vectorize()` & `replicate()` {.inv}

Built-in functions are usually vectorised, but your own (or a third-party) function may only accept **one scalar at a time**. Two loop-free helpers:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="vectorize.R"}
```{r}
# not vectorised: takes one date string
parse_it <- function(x) strsplit(x, "-")[[1]][1]
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column
# only the first is parsed
parse_it(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column
# wraps it => element-wise
parse_all <- Vectorize(parse_it)
parse_all(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column
# repeat an expression R times
replicate(4, mean(rexp(10)))
```
:::

::: {.paper-card}
**Loops without loops.** `Vectorize()` turns a scalar-only function into a vector one; `replicate(R, expr)` re-runs an expression `R` times and collects results, the function-flavoured cousin of `for`/`sapply`. Works with any expression, not just a named function.
:::

4.8 Test your functions
A good habit: check a function against a case you already know the answer to:

stopifnot(all(clamp(c(-1, 0.5, 2)) == c(0, 0.5, 1)))


Why it matters. Writing one-line assertions (stopifnot) turns “trust me” into “checked automatically”. You’ll build on this with a proper testing framework in the Reproducible Workflows course.

English   French
A course on reproducible workflows: writing Quarto documents and books, sourcing data reproducibly (including data.gouv.fr), and versioning / pinning / publishing analyses. It runs over three 3-hour sessions, each pairing slide decks with hands-on labs in Quarto (.qmd).

text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course you will be able to:

Explain what reproducibility is (and is not) along the reproducibility spectrum, and set up the full toolchain, R, Quarto and Positron, with Python via uv.
Write structured Quarto documents (YAML front matter, code cells, inline code, captions and cross-references) that a reader can follow.
Run an EDA loop: summarise and clean a dataset with {skimr}, {janitor} and {naniar}, and source open data from data.gouv.fr (or any portal) by code.
Version your data and models with {pins} and see how R and Python tooling map onto each other (uvr/renv↔︎uv, pins↔︎pins-python, vetiver↔︎vetiver-python).
Build your own Quarto book and grow it into a personal portfolio.
Version your work with git (branches, pull requests, review), pin the R version and dependencies with uvr/uv (or renv), scope randomness with {withr}, and publish to Posit Connect so others can open and reproduce it.

text:
2.1 Why version control (recap)
Your smallest reproducible unit is not a file: it’s the history of changes to a project.


Undo anything: every state of your project is recoverable.
Answer “what changed and when?”: a full log of your analysis’s evolution.
Collaborate safely: branches, PRs, review, no clobbering.
A backup that lives off-machine: your laptop dying stops being a catastrophe.



Git is the time-machine around your analysis; today we make the habit rigorous enough to share and review.

2.2 Commit, branch, push: already yours
You built these reflexes in Session 2; today we sharpen them:

git status                   # your compass: where am I?
git add <file>               # stage what you want to keep
git commit -m "message"      # snapshot with a note
git checkout -b <branch-name>   # never work on main



Commit often: small, descriptive commits beat rare mega-commits.
Never push to main: a PR is how a change reaches the shared history.



usethis::use_git() and the Positron source-control pane do all of this with clicks.

section: 2.3 Keep a branch aligned with main
text:
2.3 Keep a branch aligned with main
Before you touch a branch, fold in whatever main gained, so you never diverge silently:

git checkout main
git fetch --all --prune     # see remote changes
git pull                    # bring main up to date
git checkout <branch-name>
git merge main              # fold main into your branch


Do this before changing a branch, and your branch tracks main: conflicts largely disappear.


markdown## Keep a branch aligned with main {.inv}

Before you touch a branch, fold in whatever `main` gained, so you never diverge silently:

::: {.codewindow .bash}
```bash
git checkout main
git fetch --all --prune     # see remote changes
git pull                    # bring main up to date
git checkout <branch-name>
git merge main              # fold main into your branch
```

Do this **before** changing a branch, and your branch tracks `main`: conflicts largely disappear.

Two people change the same line, git can’t choose: it marks the file for you.

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
3.1 The moving-environment problem
Your analysis depended on package versions, which silently change:


install.packages() updates packages globally, and today’s tidyverse may differ from last month’s.
The R version itself also moves: a book may render today and break next year on a newer R.
“Works on my machine” becomes “worked on that machine, that day”.



The fix: pin the versions your project needs, committed with the code. uvr pins the packages and the R version.


markdown## The moving-environment problem {.inv}

Your analysis depended on package *versions*, which silently change:

::: {}
- `install.packages()` updates packages **globally**, and today's tidyverse may differ from last month's.
- The **R version itself** also moves: a book may render today and break next year on a newer R.
- "Works on my machine" becomes "worked on *that* machine, that day".
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
The fix: **pin** the versions your project needs, committed with the code. `uvr` pins the packages **and** the R version.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
3.2 A widely used alternative: renv
renv gives each project its own library and locks package versions with a renv.lock file. Widely used and proven, but it does not version the language: the R version is left floating.


uvr pins packages and the R version, so a fresh clone rebuilds exactly.
That one addition is what makes the whole environment reproducible, not just the packages.



Use what fits: renv for packages only, or uvr to also pin R itself. This deck follows uvr.


markdown## A widely used alternative: renv {.inv}

`renv` gives each project its own library and locks package versions with a `renv.lock` file. Widely used and proven, but it does **not** version the language: the R version is left floating.

::: {}
- `uvr` pins packages **and** the R version, so a fresh clone rebuilds exactly.
- That one addition is what makes the whole environment reproducible, not just the packages.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Use what fits: `renv` for packages only, or `uvr` to also pin R itself. This deck follows `uvr`.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
section: 3.3 uvr: pin R itself, not just packages
text:
3.3 uvr: pin R itself, not just packages
uvr wraps uv (the Python manager) so R gets the same “one engine, both languages” discipline:


uvr::init() sets up a project manifest + lockfile (a uv project).
uvr::r_install("4.6.1") installs a project-managed R version.
uvr::r_pin("4.6.1") records that version in the manifest, so it’s committed and reproducible.
uvr::add("tidyverse") adds to the manifest, regenerates the lockfile, and installs, all in one call.



r_list() shows versions; r_use() picks one for the session, r_pin() records it in the project (that’s what survives a fresh clone).


markdown## uvr: pin R itself, not just packages {.inv}

`uvr` wraps `uv` (the Python manager) so R gets the same "one engine, both languages" discipline:

::: {}
- **`uvr::init()`** sets up a project manifest + lockfile (a `uv` project).
- **`uvr::r_install("4.6.1")`** installs a project-managed R version.
- **`uvr::r_pin("4.6.1")`** records that version in the manifest, so it's **committed and reproducible**.
- **`uvr::add("tidyverse")`** adds to the manifest, regenerates the lockfile, and installs, all in one call.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
`r_list()` shows versions; `r_use()` picks one for the session, `r_pin()` records it in the project (that's what survives a fresh clone).
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
3.4 Install uvr
The companion R package from GitHub, then the uvr binary:


pak::pak("nbafrank/uvr-r")   # the uvr R package, from GitHub
uvr::install_uvr()           # installs the uvr binary (cross-platform)




One-time setup: the R package is the interface; install_uvr() puts the engine on your machine.
It relies on uv, the same tool that manages Python later in your book.



Installing the R package first, then the binary, keeps the whole uvr workflow runnable from R functions inside your project.

The companion R package from GitHub, then the `uvr` binary:

::: {.codewindow .r name="install-uvr.R"}
```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}

uvr::install_uvr()           # installs the uvr binary (cross-platform)
```
:::

::: {}
- One-time setup: the R package is the interface; `install_uvr()` puts the engine on your machine.
- It relies on `uv`, the same tool that manages Python later in your book.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Installing the R package first, then the binary, keeps the whole `uvr` workflow runnable from R functions inside your project.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
3.5 What a lockfile actually pins

uv.lock (via uvr) records each R/Python package with exact version + hashes, and pins the R version too. It stores only the recipe to rebuild them, not the packages themselves.


[r]
version = "4.6.1"

[[package]]
name = "DBI"
version = "1.3.0"
source = "cran"
raw_version = "1.3.0"
url = "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/DBI_1.3.0.tar.gz"
checksum = "md5:ce5e3153cc7395a2aac452db1099d003"


A lockfile isn’t magic; it’s an explicit, machine-readable record of what you ran with. Diff it over time to see exactly when an environment changed.


markdown## What a lockfile actually pins {.inv}

::: {.callout-desc}
`uv.lock` (via uvr) records each R/Python package with **exact version + hashes**, and pins the **R version** too. It stores only the recipe to rebuild them, not the packages themselves.
:::

::: {.codewindow name="uv.lock"}
```yaml
[r]
version = "4.6.1"

[[package]]
name = "DBI"
version = "1.3.0"
source = "cran"
raw_version = "1.3.0"
url = "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/DBI_1.3.0.tar.gz"
checksum = "md5:ce5e3153cc7395a2aac452db1099d003"
```
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
A lockfile isn't magic; it's an explicit, machine-readable record of what you ran with. Diff it over time to see exactly when an environment changed.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
4.1 Random numbers break reproducibility
Any code that uses randomness gives a different answer on every run, unless told otherwise:


Sampling, simulations, plot jitter, cross-validation splits: all change a figure or number each render.
A bare set.seed() at the top of a document leaks into the whole session and never restores it.
Result: the same .qmd renders “differently”, so a reader can’t reproduce your exact figure.



A document whose figure changes every render isn’t reproducible. Fix the seed where the randomness happens, not globally.


markdown## Random numbers break reproducibility {.inv}

Any code that uses randomness gives a different answer on every run, unless told otherwise:

::: {}
- Sampling, simulations, plot jitter, cross-validation splits: all change a figure or number each render.
- A bare `set.seed()` at the top of a document leaks into the whole session and never restores it.
- Result: the same `.qmd` renders "differently", so a reader can't reproduce your exact figure.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
A document whose figure changes every render isn't reproducible. Fix the seed **where the randomness happens**, not globally.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
4.2 Scope a seed with {withr}
{withr} sets an option for one block and restores it afterward, locally and explicitly:



withr::with_seed(2026, {
  # anything random here, for this block only
  sample(penguins$species, 5)
})


[1] Gentoo    Adelie    Chinstrap Adelie    Adelie   
Levels: Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo

# outside the block, the previous seed state is restored




withr::with_seed(seed, { ... }): set the seed for exactly that expression.
withr::local_seed(seed) inside a chunk: same idea, restored when the chunk ends.
Fix the figure inside the cell that draws it; every render then matches.



Make randomness intentional and local; your Chapter 1’s figures become exactly reproducible without leaking a seed into the session.


markdown## Scope a seed with `{withr}` {.inv}

`{withr}` sets an option for one block and restores it afterward, locally and explicitly:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="reproducible-figure.qmd"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
withr::with_seed(2026, {
  # anything random here, for this block only
  sample(penguins$species, 5)
})

# outside the block, the previous seed state is restored
```
:::

::: {}
- `withr::with_seed(seed, { ... })`: set the seed for exactly that expression.
- `withr::local_seed(seed)` inside a chunk: same idea, restored when the chunk ends.
- Fix the figure *inside the cell that draws it*; every render then matches.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Make randomness intentional and local; your Chapter 1's figures become exactly reproducible without leaking a seed into the session.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
5.1 What Posit Connect is
A published analysis is one anyone can open at a URL, with no local environment required:


Posit Connect hosts R and Python content (books, reports, apps, dashboards) behind a stable URL.
Publishing pushes your rendered book to the server; readers just open the link.
This is the “anywhere” end of the spectrum: reachable, shareable, current.



A URL is the end state of the loop: data → analysis → report → versioned → published.

5.2 Pushing a Quarto book
Rendering is local and reproducible; publishing is a one-step deploy:

quarto render          # build the book (local, reproducible)
quarto publish connect # push to Posit Connect



First publish asks you to log in / configure the server once.
Every later publish updates the same URL: your portfolio stays current.



The URL shares work outside the notebook: an employer, a teammate, or your future self all see the same, current, reproducible book.

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
section: 5.3 Proof: reproduce it on a blank machine
text:
5.3 Proof: reproduce it on a blank machine
The real test of everything this course taught: hand someone the recipe and see if the book reappears:

git clone <your-url>        # 1. get the source + history
uvr::sync()                 # 2. rebuild env + R version
quarto render               # 3. rebuild the book



Three commands, no “works on my machine”: a second person (or your future self) rebuilds your exact book.
If this doesn’t work on a fresh clone, you’ve found a reproducibility gap to fix.



Publishing gives a URL to send; clone + sync + render proves the loop closed.


markdown## Proof: reproduce it on a blank machine {.inv}

The real test of everything this course taught: hand someone the *recipe* and see if the book reappears:

::: {.codewindow .bash}
```bash
git clone <your-url>        # 1. get the source + history
uvr::sync()                 # 2. rebuild env + R version
quarto render               # 3. rebuild the book
```
:::

::: {}
- **Three commands, no "works on my machine"**: a second person (or your future self) rebuilds your exact book.
- If this *doesn't* work on a fresh clone, you've found a reproducibility gap to fix.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Publishing gives a URL to *send*; `clone + sync + render` proves the loop closed.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
5.4 The full loop, closed
Everything this course taught, in one connected picture:


Write the analysis in Quarto: source is the report.
Source the data by code: {pins} versions the fetched copy.
Version with git: every step reversible, reviewed via PRs.
Pin your environment with uvr/uv.
Deploy your model with {vetiver}, pinned like your data.
Publish to a URL: reachable and shareable.



Miss any link and the chain weakens. Keep all six and your analysis is reproducible by anyone, anywhere, at any time.


markdown## The full loop, closed {.inv}

Everything this course taught, in one connected picture:

::: {}
1. **Write** the analysis in Quarto: source *is* the report.
2. **Source** the data by code: `{pins}` versions the fetched copy.
3. **Version** with git: every step reversible, reviewed via PRs.
4. **Pin** your environment with `uvr`/`uv`.
5. **Deploy** your model with `{vetiver}`, pinned like your data.
6. **Publish** to a URL: reachable and shareable.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
Miss any link and the chain weakens. Keep all six and your analysis is reproducible by anyone, anywhere, at any time.
:::

title: My Data Science Portfolio
text:
Welcome 👋
This is your data science portfolio. Over the semester it will grow from a single exploratory data analysis (EDA) project into a collection of reproducible analyses, each versioned with git, with dependencies pinned via renv/uv, and published to a URL on Posit Connect.
The chapters in this book are:

Chapters 2 & 3, later courses: placeholders that other instructors will fill in over the semester. Leave them in place.

title: Accessing data & building the book
text:
2.1 What EDA is for

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the back-and-forth loop where you learn what the data can tell you:

Get a quick sense: shapes, types, missingness, ranges.
Look for problems: wrong types, missing values, inconsistent names/labels, outliers.
Ask & plot: small targeted plots to answer questions and surface surprises.
Record decisions: every cleaning choice documented, because a defensible choice is a feature.

EDA is iterative: you circle through 1–3 several times before any formal modelling. The output that survives into a report is the cleaned data plus the story of your decisions.


markdown## What EDA is for {.paper}

::: {.paper-card}
**Exploratory data analysis (EDA)** is the back-and-forth loop where you learn what the data can tell you:

1. **Get a quick sense**: shapes, types, missingness, ranges.
2. **Look for problems**: wrong types, missing values, inconsistent names/labels, outliers.
3. **Ask & plot**: small targeted plots to answer questions and surface surprises.
4. **Record decisions**: every cleaning choice documented, because a *defensible* choice is a feature.

EDA is *iterative*: you circle through 1–3 several times before any formal modelling. The output that survives into a report is the cleaned data **plus the story of your decisions**.
:::

title: Accessing data & building the book
text:
2.6 Dealing with missing values
Once you’ve diagnosed it, decide how to handle it. Three honest strategies; each is a documented decision, not a default:


Drop with tidyr::drop_na(): simplest, but you may lose whole columns or many rows; only acceptable when the missing cases are few and not systematically different.
Impute (fill in a plausible value): keeps all cases, but imputed values are estimated, not observed. The MissingData CRAN Task View is the curated map of R’s methods.
Keep and use na.rm = TRUE: let functions skip NA where they support it; cheapest when missingness is sparse and local.



No free lunch: dropping loses information, imputing adds an assumption, na.rm = TRUE only defers the decision. Diagnose first (skim + naniar), then choose and write down why. Where you can, make that call together with the domain experts who know what each NA actually means in this data.


markdown## Dealing with missing values {.inv}

Once you've diagnosed it, decide how to handle it. Three honest strategies; each is a *documented decision*, not a default:

::: {.spread}
1. **Drop** with `tidyr::drop_na()`: simplest, but you may lose whole **columns** or many **rows**; only acceptable when the missing cases are few and not systematically different.
2. **Impute** (fill in a plausible value): keeps all cases, but imputed values are *estimated*, not observed. The [MissingData CRAN Task View](https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/MissingData.html) is the curated map of R's methods.
3. **Keep and use `na.rm = TRUE`**: let functions skip `NA` where they support it; cheapest when missingness is sparse and local.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
No free lunch: dropping loses information, imputing adds an assumption, `na.rm = TRUE` only defers the decision. Diagnose first (skim + naniar), then choose and *write down why*. Where you can, make that call together with the **domain experts** who know what each `NA` actually means in this data.
:::

section: 3.1 Open data, anywhere in the world
text:
3.1 Open data, anywhere in the world
A reproducible analysis needs data it can re-fetch by code, and open-data portals everywhere provide exactly that:


France: data.gouv.fr, thousands of public datasets, license-aware.
Your own country: nearly every government runs an official open-data portal (data.gov… for the US, Canada, UK, Germany, and many more).
The rule is the same wherever you look: a dataset you can fetch programmatically is a dataset your analysis can re-produce.



The reproducible move: don’t download a dataset by hand; write code that sources it, so the analysis is re-runnable and the provenance (publisher + URL) is in the document.

A reproducible analysis needs data it can **re-fetch by code**, and open-data portals everywhere provide exactly that:

::: {}

- **France**: [data.gouv.fr](https://www.data.gouv.fr), thousands of public datasets, **license-aware**.
- **Your own country**: nearly every government runs an official open-data portal (data.gov… for the US, Canada, UK, Germany, and many more).
- **The rule is the same wherever you look**: a dataset you can fetch *programmatically* is a dataset your analysis can re-produce.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
The reproducible move: don't *download* a dataset by hand; write code that *sources* it, so the analysis is re-runnable and the provenance (publisher + URL) is in the document.
