text:
3.2 {rdatagouv}: the French portal from R (an option)
Because we teach from l’ENSAI, data.gouv.fr is a natural default. Its thousands of public datasets trend toward the public, transport, environment and culture topics the French job market cares about, and they’re license-aware, so the dataset you showcase is safe to publish. {rdatagouv} (maintained by your instructor) wraps it:

Why a natural pick: pick a topic you care about that a future recruiter would also find compelling once your portfolio is online. Whatever you choose, {rdatagouv} is an option, not a requirement: any portal you can query with a URL (e.g. download.file()) works just as well for reproducibility.


markdown## [{rdatagouv}](https://astamm.github.io/rdatagouv/): the French portal from R (an option) {.inv}

Because we teach from l'ENSAI, **data.gouv.fr** is a natural default. Its thousands of public datasets trend toward the **public, transport, environment and culture** topics the French job market cares about, and they're **license-aware**, so the dataset you showcase is safe to publish. [{rdatagouv}](https://astamm.github.io/rdatagouv/) (maintained by your instructor) wraps it:

```{r}
#| label: rdatagouv
#| eval: false
library(rdatagouv)
# search the FRENCH portal for a topic
search_datasets("population", type = "dataset")
# get metadata + resource URLs for a dataset you found
dataset <- get_dataset("my-dataset-slug")
dataset$resources
```

::: {.callout-desc}
Why a natural pick: pick a **topic you care about** that a future recruiter would also find compelling once your portfolio is online. Whatever you choose, [{rdatagouv}](https://astamm.github.io/rdatagouv/) is an *option, not a requirement*: any portal you can query with a URL (e.g. `download.file()`) works just as well for reproducibility.
:::

title: Accessing data & building the book
text:
3.3 Fetching any portal by URL
Whatever portal you choose, the reproducible core is the same: a URL your code downloads:


download.file() is portal-agnostic: it doesn’t care whether the URL points at data.gouv.fr or your home country’s portal.
Pair it with a provenance sentence (dataset, publisher, URL, license) so a reader can find and trust the source.
Some portals ship an R/Python client ({rdatagouv} here): a convenience, never a requirement.



Live block (≈10 min). Together: rdatagouv::dg_find_datasets(q = "climat", schema_only = TRUE) and browse one non-French portal (e.g. your home country’s). Both approaches collapse to the same thing: a URL to download by code.


markdown## Fetching any portal by URL {.inv}

Whatever portal you choose, the reproducible core is the same: a URL your code downloads:

```{r}
#| label: fetch-url
#| eval: false
url <- "https://…/my-open-dataset.csv"   # any open-data portal, any country
download.file(url, "data/my-data.csv")   # a RE-RUNNABLE line of code
```

::: {}

- **`download.file()` is portal-agnostic**: it doesn't care whether the URL points at data.gouv.fr or your home country's portal.
- Pair it with a **provenance sentence** (dataset, publisher, URL, license) so a reader can *find* and *trust* the source.
- Some portals ship an R/Python client ([{rdatagouv}](https://astamm.github.io/rdatagouv/) here): a convenience, never a requirement.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
**Live block (≈10 min).** Together: `rdatagouv::dg_find_datasets(q = "climat", schema_only = TRUE)` *and* browse one non-French portal (e.g. your home country's). Both approaches collapse to the same thing: a URL to download by code.
:::

title: Accessing data & building the book
section: 3.4 Data that ships as an R package
text:
3.4 Data that ships as an R package
Not every dataset needs a portal: many ship inside an R (or Python) package, and that’s reproducible too. You’ve used one already, palmerpenguins::penguins.


A versioned package is reproducible data: the package is properly released and versioned on CRAN (or PyPI), and its docs and provenance ship with it.
Because it’s a package, your environment manager (uvr/uv) can lock its exact version, so a re-render gets the same data today and next year.
Good examples: {gapminder}, {nycflights13}, {babynames}, {Lahman} (baseball), {tidycensus}, {rdatagouv}’s returned data.



A packaged dataset is the ultimate reproducible source: one line to load, an immutable version, documented. That’s why today’s analysis can trust palmerpenguins without a portal or a download.file().

title: Accessing data & building the book
Accessing data & building the book
text:
4.1 The (dis)appearing data problem
Last session you met “the (dis)appearing data”: a fetched file can change or vanish the moment it’s off the portal:


A portal updates a dataset: your analysis was based on the old version.
A raw URL 404s a year later, and your “reproducible” document can’t re-run.
Even locally, data/my-data.csv can be overwritten, and git alone doesn’t version the cached copy well if you don’t commit it.



{pins} closes that gap: version your data the way git versions your code, so a re-render gets the same data a reader expects, not whatever is live today.


markdown## The (dis)appearing data problem {.inv}

Last session you met "the (dis)appearing data": a fetched file can *change* or *vanish* the moment it's off the portal:

::: {}

- A portal updates a dataset: your analysis was based on the **old version**.
- A raw URL 404s a year later, and your "reproducible" document can't re-run.
- Even locally, `data/my-data.csv` can be overwritten, and git alone doesn't version the *cached* copy well if you don't commit it.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
[{pins}](https://pins.rstudio.com) closes that gap: **version your data** the way git versions your code, so a re-render gets the *same* data a reader expects, not whatever is live today.
:::

title: Accessing data & building the book
section: 4.2 {pins}: pin data to a versioned board
text:
4.2 {pins}: pin data to a versioned board
{pins} stores a data object on a board and records who wrote what, when:


# a folder board that KEEPS HISTORY (versioned = TRUE)
bd <- pins::board_folder(path = "pins/", versioned = TRUE)

# fetch open data once, then pin it:
dat <- readr::read_csv("https://…/my-open-dataset.csv")
pins::pin_write(board = bd, x = dat, name = "my-dataset")        # snapshot it, versioned & hashed

# later re-reads get the PINNED copy, reproducibly:
pins::pin_read(board = bd, name = "my-dataset")



pin_write() snapshots the data and records the version + hash; pin_read() returns that exact snapshot. Re-render → same data, every time.


markdown## [{pins}](https://pins.rstudio.com): pin data to a versioned board {.inv}

[{pins}](https://pins.rstudio.com) stores a data object on a **board** and records **who wrote what, when**:

::: {.codewindow .r name="pins.R"}
```{r}
#| label: pins-setup
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
# a folder board that KEEPS HISTORY (versioned = TRUE)
bd <- pins::board_folder(path = "pins/", versioned = TRUE)

# fetch open data once, then pin it:
dat <- readr::read_csv("https://…/my-open-dataset.csv")
pins::pin_write(board = bd, x = dat, name = "my-dataset")        # snapshot it, versioned & hashed

# later re-reads get the PINNED copy, reproducibly:
pins::pin_read(board = bd, name = "my-dataset")
```
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
`pin_write()` snapshots the data and records the **version + hash**; `pin_read()` returns that exact snapshot. Re-render → same data, every time.
:::

title: Accessing data & building the book
text:
4.3 Where the versioned copy lives
A board is just a folder (or a service), and it’s fully inspectable:


pin_list(board): what’s been pinned.
pin_versions(board, "my-dataset"): every snapshot, with hashes and dates.
pin_read(board, "my-dataset", version = "…"): roll back to an older snapshot.



The pinned pins/ folder is committed alongside your code, so the exact data your analysis used is reproducible forever, independent of portal changes or broken URLs.


markdown## Where the versioned copy lives {.inv}

A board is just a folder (or a service), and it's fully inspectable:

::: {.spread}
- `pin_list(board)`: what's been pinned.
- `pin_versions(board, "my-dataset")`: every snapshot, with hashes and dates.
- `pin_read(board, "my-dataset", version = "…")`: roll back to an older snapshot.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}
The pinned `pins/` folder is committed alongside your code, so the *exact data* your analysis used is reproducible forever, independent of portal changes or broken URLs.
:::

title: Accessing data & building the book
text:
4.4 Fetch once, pin, analyse
A reproducible data workflow in three deliberate steps:


Fetch the open data by URL: provenance recorded.
Pin it with pin_write(): versioned & hashed on a local board.
Analyse from the pinned copy (pin_read()): stable no matter what happens upstream.

markdown## Fetch once, pin, analyse {.inv}

::: {.spread}

3. **Analyse from the pinned copy** (`pin_read()`): stable no matter what happens upstream.
:::

::: {.callout-desc .fragment}

5.1 Git in one habit
You version your data with {pins}; you version your code with git, one round at a time:

git status             # your compass: where am I?

git commit -m "msg"   # snapshot with a note
git push              # send the snapshot to GitHub



usethis::use_git() turns the folder into a git repo; the Positron git pane is the clickable version of the loop.
Commit often: small, descriptive commits beat rare mega-commits; git status is your compass.



Version your code the way you just versioned your data. add → commit → push is the whole habit; everything else is dress-up.

Local history is half the story; a remote (GitHub) makes it durable and shareable:

text:
5.4 Branches: keep main always-working
A branch is a second history you can work on without touching main:

git checkout -b eda-chapter-1          # make + switch to a branch
# work on it
git commit -am "add chapter 1"         # stage + snapshot
git push -u origin eda-chapter-1       # share the branch early
# each time you re-work it, re-align with main:
git checkout main && git fetch --all --prune && git pull
git checkout eda-chapter-1 && git merge main



Mirror how you actually work: try an idea on a branch, keep it if it works; main stays always-working.
In the Positron git pane, the branch menu creates and switches branches.



Re-align with main often so conflicts stay small; never push to main directly (Session 3’s pull request decides what merges).


8.1 A report is read, not just rendered
Your EDA will be read by other humans, instructors, classmates, future employers. Write to them:


Structure signals intent: question, data, cleaning, results, findings.
Captions do the explaining: a reader should grasp a figure from its caption before reading your prose.
Say what you found and what you didn’t: honest limits are credibility.
Keep code in service of the story: the code shows how; the prose says why it matters.



The reproducibility narrative: because everything is code and captioned, a stranger re-rendering your .qmd both trusts and reproduces your work. That’s the product.

Setup your machine · Reproducible Workflows
text:
English   French
This page covers the parts of the toolchain specific to the Reproducible Workflows course: Quarto, Python (via uv), git, and publishing. It assumes you already have R, Positron and the core R packages from the companion Setup · common page.

title: Setup your machine · Reproducible Workflows
text:
1. Install Quarto
Quarto is our open-source scientific and technical publishing system. It turns .qmd documents (and RevealJS slides!) into polished HTML, PDF, and more.

Download: https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/

Check it works:
quarto --version   # e.g. 1.10.x

title: Setup your machine · Reproducible Workflows
text:
2. Version control with git
Everything in this course is versioned with git. Install it first, then set your identity.
git --version                    # e.g. 2.4x.x
For Windows users, follow https://happygitwithr.com/install-git. On macOS/Linux, git usually ships with the OS or the Xcode command-line tools.
Your git identity should match the account you use on GitHub, where your repositories will be hosted. If you do not have one yet, create a free account at https://github.com. Then set the same name and email you used there as your global git identity:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
If you are already working in R, usethis::use_git_config() walks you through setting these same values; usethis and gitcreds are handy companions for all the Session 2/3 git work (see https://happygitwithr.com/hello-git).
The required R packages for the git work are usethis and gitcreds, both installed in Setup · common. Reference guide: https://happygitwithr.com/.

Personal access tokens (PAT)
You need to grant Positron permissions to act on the behalf of your GitHub account. The recommended way nowadays is to create a personal access token (PAT) on GitHub and register it in Positron.
While you can create it directly from the GitHub interface online and then register it manually, usethis makes it one command:
usethis::create_github_token()
This command requests to open a web browser page for PAT creation with appropriate options already checked.

Proceed with creating the PAT.
Copy the PAT to clipboard with the button.

Then, back in Positron, do:
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
Follow the instructions, paste the PAT and validate. git push and usethis::use_github() then authenticate automatically.


Structure your work and push to GitHub
Take the habit of creating a dedicated folder for each project and opening it in Positron as working directory, then initialize version control on it:
usethis::use_git()
In Positron you can access the Git pane in the left sidebar. Once your project is committed locally, push a remote copy to GitHub:
usethis::use_github()

title: Setup your machine · Reproducible Workflows
text:
3. Publishing with Posit Connect
Session 3 reports are published to Posit Connect, the server that puts your work live at a URL. There is nothing to install, but you do need an account on the server: a free-tier account is sufficient for this course. The instructor will hand out the sign-up URL in Session 3. Then you publish from inside Quarto with quarto publish connect.

title: Setup your machine · Reproducible Workflows
section: 4. Pinning a whole project with uvr
text:
4. Pinning a whole project with uvr
For the Reproducible Workflows course you pin a whole project, not just one machine: the R version and every package’s version, so the project re-runs identically next year on another machine. That is what uvr does. It is a thin wrapper that lets R use uv (the same Rust project manager that drives the Python setup below). Install it from GitHub, then install its binary:
pak::pak("nbafrank/uvr-r")   # the uvr companion R package
uvr::install_uvr()           # installs the uvr binary (cross-platform)
Inside a project folder (uvr::init()), uvr manages a project-local R (uvr::r_install("4.6.1"), uvr::r_pin("4.6.1")) and adds packages to a manifest + lockfile with uvr::add("tidyverse"). So uvr is not only about which R version you run: it installs and pins every dependency behind a lockfile. That makes it the project-scoped alternative to the r2u / install.packages() / pak::pak() routes in Setup · common. Use those to get R and packages working machine-wide; reach for uvr once you are inside a real project you need to reproduce.

title: Setup your machine · Reproducible Workflows
text:
5. Setup Python (optional)
In Positron:

Open the palette with the keyboard shortcut CMD + SHIFT + P;
Search for Python: install Python via uv and proceed.

More at https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-07-08_positron-uv/

title: Setup your machine · Reproducible Workflows
text:
6. Install Python packages (optional)
uv is an extremely fast Python package and project manager, written in Rust.
You can easily install Python packages in dedicated virtual environments with uv. For example, to install the pandas and numpy packages, run in the Positron-integrated terminal:
uv init example
# Initialized project `example` at `/home/user/example`
uv add pandas numpy
More details can be found on the website.

title: The tractoverse
text:
The brain’s white matter





Diffusion MRI probes water motion in tissue at the micron scale.

Axons restrict diffusion along their axis → anisotropy
Magnetic field gradient attenuates the MR signal → diffusion-weighted images
Voxel-level diffusion model → local fiber orientation and tissue properties

Tractography follows these orientations across voxels to reconstruct 3-D fiber trajectories which carry microstructural information.

title: The tractoverse
text:
fiber — S7 data structures

The backbone of the tractoverse. Like tibble is to the tidyverse. Three S7 classes:




streamline — one tract @points (\(P \times 3\) matrix) @point_data (list of length-\(P\) numeric vectors) @streamline_data (list of scalars)


bundle — collection of streamlines @streamlines (list of \(S\) streamlines) @streamline_data (list of length-\(S\) numeric vectors) @bundle_data (list of scalars)


bundle_set — multi-subject / multi-session @bundles (list of \(B\) bundles) @bundle_data (list of length-\(B\) numeric vectors) @set_data (list of scalars)




Data lifting and subsetting ✅ @streamline_data common to all streamlines in a bundle → lifted to @streamline_data of the bundle; ✅ @bundle_data common to all bundles in a set → lifted to @set_data of the bundle set. ✅ Upon subsetting, lifted data is propagated down to the lower-level objects.

title: The tractoverse
text:
fiber — quick start
library(fiber)

t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 50)

# Build a helix streamline
sl <- streamline(
  points     = cbind(X = cos(t), Y = sin(t), Z = t / (2 * pi)),
  point_data = list(FA = runif(50, 0.3, 0.9))
)
sl
#> ── Object of class `fiber::streamline()` with 50 points. ──
#>  • Point attributes: FA
#>  • Streamline attributes: none

# Geometry on streamlines
get_curvilinear_length(sl)   #> [1] 6.36
get_sinuosity(sl)            #> [1] 6.36

# Build a bundle and reparametrize
b <- bundle(lapply(1:10, \(i) reparametrize(sl, n_points = 20L)))
b
#> ── Object of class `fiber::bundle()` with 10 streamlines [20-20 pts/sl] ──

# Multi-subject bundle set
bs <- bundle_set(list("sub-01" = b, "sub-02" = b))
bs
#> ── Object of class `fiber::bundle_set()` with 2 bundles [10-10 sl/bundle] ──

title: The tractoverse
text:
midi — microstructure simulation

Microstructure Information from Diffusion Imaging. Simulate the MR signal attenuation from parametric tissue models — used to validate tractography algorithms and design experiments.




Taxonomy of compartments:

Restricted (cylinders, spheres): model axons
Hindered (tensors): model extra-axonal space
Free (isotropic): model CSF

Each compartment is an R6 object with method $get_signal().



# ------- Define a cylinder compartment (axon model) -------
restr <- VanGelderenCompartment$new(
  radius      = 0.5,  # µm
  diffusivity = 3     # µm²/ms
)
cyl <- CylinderCompartment$new(
  axis                   = c(0, 0, 1),
  restricted_compartment = restr
)
# ------- Query parameters -------
cyl$get_parameters()
#> $CylinderRadius      [1] 0.5
#> $CylinderDiffusivity [1] 3
# ------- Compute signal attenuation -------
cyl$get_signal(
  small_delta = 30, big_delta = 30,
  G = 0.04, direction = c(0, 0, 1)
)
#> [1] 0.002063

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Problem formulation
Functional data on \(L^2(D) \cup \mathcal{C}^0(D)\), where \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^d\).
A null hypothesis \(H_0^t\) which is true on a subset \(D_0 \subseteq D\) and false on \(D_1 = D \setminus D_0\).
Aim: estimate \(D_0\) by testing locally \(H_0^t\) against \(H_1^t\).






\[
\small{

Pointwise testing
Straightforward solution: a statistical test for each point of the domain









P-values from permutations of residuals (Freedman and Lane 1983).











Multiplicity issue: no control of \(\mathbb{P}\)(no false rejection).











Multiplicity issue: no control of \(\mathbb{P}\)(no false rejection).

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
What is the multiplicity issue?






Definition 1 (Familywise error rate)


The familywise error rate (FWER) is the probability of making at least one false rejection among a family of tests.









Problem


For \(m\) stochastically independent tests at level \(\alpha\), among which \(m_0\) are true null hypotheses, the FWER can be expressed as: \[
\text{FWER} = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^{m_0} \to 1 \quad \text{as } m_0 \to \infty \text{ when } \alpha \in (0,1].
\]

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Functional control of the FWER






Definition 2 (Weak control of the FWER)


A procedure for locally testing – over the domain \(D\) – a null hypothesis \(H_0^t\) against an alternative \(H_1^t\), \(\forall t \in D\), is provided with weak control of the FWER if the adjusted p-value \(\widetilde{p}(t)\) is such that for all \(\alpha \in (0,1)\):
\[
H_0^{D_\phantom{0}} \mbox{ is true } \Longrightarrow \mathbb{P}(\exists t \in D : \widetilde{p}(t) \le \alpha) \le \alpha.
\]

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Functional control of the FWER






Definition 3 (Strong control of the FWER)


A procedure for locally testing – over the domain \(D\) – a null hypothesis \(H_0^t\) against an alternative \(H_1^t\), \(\forall t \in D\), is provided with strong control of the FWER if the adjusted p-value \(\widetilde{p}(t)\) is such that:
\[
\forall A \subseteq D \text{ s.t. } H_0^A \text{ is true } \Rightarrow \mathbb{P}(\exists t \in A : \widetilde{p}(t) \le \alpha) \le \alpha, \quad \text{for all } \alpha \in (0,1).
\]

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Closed Testing Procedure in MDA






Definition 4: Closed testing (Marcus et al. 1976)


The closed testing procedure is a multiple testing method where a null hypothesis \(H_0^{(i)}\) is rejected at level \(\alpha\) if every intersection hypothesis that contains \(H_0^{(i)}\) is rejected at level \(\alpha\).

Global Testing 1






Predefined family \(\mathcal{S} = \{D\}\)\(\mathcal{S} = \{D\}\)
Weak control of the FWER
No domain selection (i.e., \(\widetilde{p}(t)\)\(\widetilde{p}(t)\) \(\equiv \mathrm{const}\))
Computationally efficient (one test)

Hall and Tajvidi (2002), Pini, Stamm, et al. (2018) .

Borel-Wise Testing 1






Predefined family \(\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{B}(D)\)\(\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{B}(D)\)
Strong control of the FWER
No domain selection (i.e., \(\widetilde{p}(t)\)\(\widetilde{p}(t)\) \(\equiv \mathrm{const} \ge \max \{p(t) : t \in D\}\))
Computationally inefficient (\(2^p\) tests for a grid of \(p\) points)

Marcus et al. (1976) .

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Partition-Closed Testing 1






Predefined family \(\mathcal{S} = \sigma(\{S_j\}_{j=1}^J)\)\(\mathcal{S} = \sigma(\{S_j\}_{j=1}^J)\), with \(\{S_j\}_{j=1}^J\) a partition of \(D\)
Strong between-set control, weak within-set control of the FWER
Subset selection (i.e., \(\widetilde{p}(t)\)\(\widetilde{p}(t)\) \(= p^{S_j}\) for \(t \in S_j\))
Computationally inefficient if \(J\) is high (\(2^J\) tests)

Vsevolozhskaya et al. (2013), Vsevolozhskaya et al. (2014) .

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Partition-Closed Testing 1
























Predefined family \(\mathcal{S} = \sigma(\{S_j\}_{j=1}^J)\)\(\mathcal{S} = \sigma(\{S_j\}_{j=1}^J)\), with \(\{S_j\}_{j=1}^J\) a partition of \(D\)
For \(J\) going to infinity, PCT = BWT:

\(\lim_{J \to \infty}\) \(\widetilde{p}_J^\mathrm{PCT}(t)\)\(\widetilde{p}_J^\mathrm{PCT}(t)\) \(=\) \(\widetilde{p}^\mathrm{BWT}(t)\)\(\widetilde{p}^\mathrm{BWT}(t)\).
Vsevolozhskaya et al. (2013), Vsevolozhskaya et al. (2014) .

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Interval-Wise Testing 1






Predefined family \(\mathcal{S} = \{[t_1^l, t_1^r] \times \dots \times [t_d^l, t_d^r] : t_i^l \le t_i^r, i \in [\![ 1,d ]\!] \}\)\(\mathcal{S} = \{[t_1^l, t_1^r] \times \dots \times [t_d^l, t_d^r] : t_i^l \le t_i^r, i \in [\![ 1,d ]\!] \}\)
Strong control if \(D_0\) is a Cartesian product of intervals, weak control otherwise;
Domain selection (i.e., \(\widetilde{p}^\text{IWT}(t)\)\(\widetilde{p}^\text{IWT}(t)\) is a continuous function)
Computationally inefficient for large \(d\) (\(p^{2d}\) tests)

Pini and Vantini (2017), Pini, Vantini, et al. (2018), Abramowicz et al. (2018) .

title: Domain selection and familywise error rate for functional data: A unified framework
text:
Threshold-Wise Testing 1






Data-driven family \(\mathcal{S} = \{ \{t : p(t) \le s\}, \{t : p(t) > s\}, s \in [0,1] \}\)\(\mathcal{S} = \{ \{t : p(t) \le s\}, \{t : p(t) > s\}, s \in [0,1] \}\)
Strong control asymptotically, finite weak control
Domain selection (i.e., \(\widetilde{p}^\text{TWT}(t)\)\(\widetilde{p}^\text{TWT}(t)\) is a continuous function)
Computationally efficient for any \(d\) (\(2m\) tests, with \(m\) the discretization step of \([0,1]\))

Abramowicz et al. (2023) .

Unit quaternion


A unit quaternion \(\mathbf{q} = (q_w, q_x, q_y, q_z)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4\) encodes a rotation of angle \(\theta\) around the axis \(\mathbf{u}\) as: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{q} &= q_w + q_x \mathbf{i} + q_y \mathbf{j} + q_z \mathbf{k} \\
&= \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right) + (u_x \mathbf{i} + u_y \mathbf{j} + u_z \mathbf{k}) \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right),
\end{aligned}
\] with \(\mathbf{i}^2 = \mathbf{j}^2 = \mathbf{k}^2 = \mathbf{i} \mathbf{j} \mathbf{k} = -1\).





Raw data collected by the eGait device:

Represents the hip rotation over time (Drouin 2022);
In the form of a unit quaternion time series.

Definition 1 (Smooth manifold) A smooth or differentiable manifold is a topological space that locally resembles linear space.






Figure 5: A manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) and the vector space \(T_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{M}\) tangent at point \(\mathcal{X}\). The velocity element \(\dot{\mathcal{X}}\) does not belong to the manifold but to the tangent space (Sola et al. 2018).

title: R, un catalyseur d’interdisciplinarité
text:
Lie groups



Definition 2 (Group) A group is a set \(\mathcal{G}\), with composition operation \(\circ\), that, for elements \(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{Z} \in \mathcal{G}\), satisfies the following axioms:

Closure under \(\circ\): \(\mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{Y} \in \mathcal{G}\)
Identity \(\mathcal{E}\): \(\mathcal{E} \circ \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{E} = \mathcal{X}\)
Inverse \(\mathcal{X}^{-1}\): \(\mathcal{X}^{-1} \circ \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{X}^{-1} = \mathcal{E}\)
Associativity: \((\mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{Y}) \circ \mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X} \circ (\mathcal{Y} \circ \mathcal{Z})\)




Definition 3 (Lie group) A Lie group is a smooth manifold whose elements satisfy the group axioms.







Figure 6: Representation of a Lie group and its Lie algebra. The Lie algebra \(T_\mathcal{E} \mathcal{M}\) (red plane) is the tangent space to the Lie group \(\mathcal{M}\) (blue sphere) at the identity \(\mathcal{E}\) (Sola et al. 2018).

The Lie group \(S^3\) of unit quaternions






Figure 7: The \(S^3\) manifold is a unit 3-sphere (blue) in the 4-space of quaternions \(\mathbb{H}\), where the unit quaternions \(\mathbf{q}^\star \mathbf{q} = 1\) live. The Lie algebra is the space of pure imaginary quaternions \(ix + jy + kz \in \mathbb{H}_p\), isomorphic to the hyperplane \(\mathbb{R}^3\) (red grid), and any other tangent space \(T S^3\) is also isomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) (Sola et al. 2018).



Vectors \(\mathbf{x} = (0, x_1, x_2, x_3) = 0 + ix_1 + jx_2 + kx_3\) rotate in 3D space by an angle \(\theta\) around the unit axis \(\mathbf{u}\) through the double quaternion product \(\mathbf{x}^\prime = \mathbf{q} \mathbf{x} \mathbf{q}^\star\).

text:
Elastic shape metrics

The SRVF space is by construction invariant by translation:

\[
d(\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2) = \left\| \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2 \right\|_{L^2} \quad \mbox{and} \quad d(\mathbf{t}_1 + \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{t}_2 + \mathbf{x}_0) = d(\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2)
\]

We can use suitable metrics to add further geometric invariants:








Geometric invariant
Distance (all isometric)




Warping
\(d(\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2) = \min_{\gamma \in \Gamma} \left\| \mathbf{v}_1 - (\mathbf{v}_2 \circ \gamma) \sqrt{\dot{\gamma}} \right\|_{L^2}\)


Orientation
\(d(\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2) = \min_{R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)} \left\| \mathbf{v}_1 - R \mathbf{v}_2 \right\|_{L^2}\)


Scale
\(d(\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2) = \left\| \frac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|_{L_2}} - \frac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|_{L_2}} \right\|_{L^2}\)



\[
\Gamma = \{ \gamma : [0,1] \to [0,1] | \gamma(0) = 0, \gamma(1) = 1, 0 < \dot{\gamma} < +\infty \}
\]

title: squat
text:
Rotation data







Unit quaternions


Unit quaternions are hypercomplex numbers (Hamilton) of unit norm that encode a 3D rotation via:
\[
\mathbf{q} = (q_w, q_x, q_y, q_z) = \left(\cos \frac{\theta}{2}, i v_x \sin \frac{\theta}{2}, j v_y \sin \frac{\theta}{2}, k v_z \sin \frac{\theta}{2}  \right),
\]
where:

\(\mathbf{v} = (v_x, v_y, v_z)^\top\) and \(\theta\) are resp. axis and angle of rotation,
\(i\), \(j\) and \(k\) are s.t. \(i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = −1\) and \(\| q \| = 1\).

title: squat
text:
Mathematics of quaternions










Algebra of unit quaternion


Usual addition and scalar multiplication do not apply.
\[
\| q_1 + q_2 \| \ne 1 \quad \| \lambda q \| \ne 1
\]
Multiplication follows Hamilton’s rule:
\[
\mathbf{p} \mathbf{q} = \begin{pmatrix}
p_w q_w + p_x q_x + p_y q_y + p_z q_z \\
p_w q_x - p_x q_w - p_y q_z + p_z q_y \\
p_w q_y + p_x q_z - p_y q_w - p_z q_x \\
p_w q_z - p_x q_y + p_y q_x - p_z q_w
\end{pmatrix}
\]

title: squat
text:
Wrappin’ up
The squat package currently allows you to analyze time series of 3D object orientations

seamlessly for clustering and PCA;
with a bit of extra work for other analyses (e.g. regression/prediction) via the provided exp() and log() maps.

Do not hesitate to create an issue on the GitHub repository if you want other statistical analyses to be implemented in the same way as the clustering and PCA.

title: The Large P small n Project
text:
Overview
The Large \(P\) small \(n\) project – or \(Pn\) project for short – aims at providing inferential tools for the statistical analysis of data sets characterized by a large number of features observed on a small number of sample units, often referred to in the literature as high-dimensional multivariate data. During the last decades, this kind of data have become very common in many active fields of research, such as medicine, engineering, climatology, and economics. The first application of the newly developed inferential procedures will be the statistical analysis of the brain vascular system with the final goal of detecting statistical associations between geometry, topology, hemodynamic space-time patterns and the onset and rupture of cerebral aneurysms.

title: The Large P small n Project
text:
Scopes
During the last decades, the phenomena investigated in many active fields of research (e.g., medicine, engineering, climatology, economics) have become increasingly complex, providing large amount of information to be statistically analyzed. Consequently, the typical data set - provided by scientific experiments or observations - has drifted from being characterized by a number \(n\) of sample units much larger than the number \(p\) of variables (small \(p\) large \(n\) data), to its large \(p\) small \(n\) counterpart (i.e. data sets characterized by a number \(p\) of variables much larger than the number \(n\) of sample units).
Inferential statistical analysis of traditional small \(p\) large \(n\) data often relies on the well known central limit theorem: this theorem, under very weak assumptions (i.e. independence and identical distribution of the observations) guarantees the reliability of many commonly used inferential statistical procedures (e.g. hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, …) when the number \(n\) of sample units is far larger than the number \(p\) of variables.
The Large \(p\) Small \(n\) project aims at providing a new \(p\)-asymptotic central limit theorem (i.e. \(p\) goes to infinity with \(n\) finite) enabling inferential analysis of modern large \(p\) small \(n\) data: both in the \(p\)-discrete case (random vectors with a very large number of components) and in the \(p\)-continuous case (random functions). No reliable inferential results are nowadays available to this purpose.
The achievement of such results and the development of the consequent inferential tools (that are going to be jointly carried out by the Department of Mathematics of Politecnico di Milano and by the IRISA Institut de Recherche en Informatique et Systèmes Aléatoires, Rennes, France) will involve expertise in advanced fields of mathematics (theory of stochastic processes, multivariate statistics and data analysis, functional real analysis, and operator theory). In spite of this, the present project aims at providing tools that will be reasonably simple and readily usable by any member of the scientific community (an automated R library and a Microsoft Excel macro are expected to be provided at the end of the project).
The first application of the newly developed inferential procedures will be the statistical analysis of the brain vascular system of different groups of patients hospitalized at the Neuroradiology Department of Niguarda Ca’ Granda Hospital – Milan. The final goal of the analysis is the detection of statistical associations between geometry, topology, hemodynamic space-time patterns and the onset and rupture of cerebral aneurysms. These associations, if found, would help neurosurgeons in the choice of the patient’s best treatment, possibly decreasing the mortality rate due to both this pathology and to its medical treatments.
Raw data collected at the Neuroradiology Department of Niguarda Ca’ Granda Hospital – Milan are going to be preprocessed by the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science of Emory University – Atlanta, GA, USA.

title: The Large P small n Project
text:
State of the project
The Pn project was a \(2\)-year project that started in november 2011 until december 2013 and is now over. The project partners were Politecnico di Milano, Unversity of Rennes I and Emory University. The project funder was the 5x1000 donation program of the Politecnico di Milano. As for the team members, here is what they became since the end of the project:

Simone is now Full Professor in Statistics at the Politecnico di Milano, Italy.
Tiziano is now a research scientist at Siemens Corporation, Princeton, USA.
I am now a research engineer, expert in statistical information, at the National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), France.
Alessia is now Associate Professor in Statistics at the Università del Sacro Cuore, Milano, Italy.

title: The H\(^2\)C Project
text:
Objectives
This is a single-person research project of which I am the PI. The main objectives of the project are:

To develop new mathematical methods for estimating brain tissue microstructure and structural connectivity from diffusion MRI data;
To develop new statistical methods for comparing populations of complex mathematical objects belonging to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, with applications to the study of aneurysms and various brain pathologies.

title: The H\(^2\)C Project
text:
Results

Scientific research
The results of the research activity have been published in three scientific papers and several conference presentations (two of which were invited).


Supervision
I have co-supervised 5 master theses on topics at the frontier between statistical analysis of functional data and neuroimaging and 2 PhD students, one of whom (Riccardo Pascuzzo) spent a period at University College London (UCL) to work on the statistical analysis of MRI and the other (Ilenia Lovato) is working on the development of statistical inference methods for the analysis of populations of networks and spent a period at Harvard Medical School (HMS).


Softwares
I have written two R packages fdahotelling and fiber. The first one includes an implementation of inferential tools for the study of populations of functions. The second one includes methods for the statistical representation of brain white matter tracts. I have also written the R package nevada for the statistical analysis of network data which is on CRAN.


National and international collaborations
I have created and maintained strong collaborations between our Department of Mathematics and other research centers of excellence:

INRIA Rennes, France: several publications in collaboration with the Empenn (formerly, Visages) team, exchange of master students;
Harvard Medical School, USA: several publications in collaboration with the Computational Radiology Lab (CRL) led by Prof. Simon K. Warfield, intership of Ilenia Lovato at CRL, Harvard-Polimi agreement;
University College London, England: Internship of Riccardo Pascuzzo in the Microstructure Imaging Group (MIG) led by Prof. Daniel Alexander;
Carlo Besta Neurological Institute: several projects between MOX and the Institute. One of our PhD students should be hired by the Institute as a post- doc via an H2020. I am also part of the MOX-GMB project in collaboration with the Institute for the study of glioblastoma (a type of tumor) managed by Prof. Ciarletta. I am involved in the design of MRI sequences and post-processing of images.
